26 Black Friday Deals on Editor-Tested Ropes, Packs, Shoes, and More

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

(Photo: Courtesy Black Diamond, Ocun, Scarpa, and Trango).

In a recent development, in this economy, climbers can’t afford to pass up a good deal. Unless you’re crafty and have a sewing machine—not to mention a home welding kit—we imagine there are a few things you could use. Most of the deals we outline below can be found at Backcountry, at REI, and at specific manufacturers like Black Diamond.

Backcountry launched its Black Friday Sale early on November 20, with deals up to 60% off. We found some of the best deals on climbing shoes there. Competing outdoor retailer REI launched a Holiday Sale on November 13 with up to 25% off discounts that we expect to endure through Cyber Monday. However, if you’re shopping in person, keep in mind that the co-op is closed on Black Friday itself for its annual #OptOutside campaign.

According to recent reports, on the brand side, Black Diamond has been running an outlet sale more or less all month with up to 50% off past styles (mostly apparel, but some hardgoods). Black Diamond is offering a Holiday Sale through November 30 with up to 25% off. On November 27, it shifts into deeper Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals of up to 60% off. We found some steals on editor-recommended gear at BD you won’t want to miss.

As you head into the discount madness, here are a couple Black Friday/Cyber Monday shopping tips for climbers:.

Looking to build out your climbing shoe quiver? Is your go-to pair beyond the point of resole or repair? Ready to graduate to a more performance-oriented design? This is your moment. You may be thinking: But I’m not going to be climbing much for the next few months. I’ll just wait.

According to recent reports, real ones know that would be a grave error. Come February or March, you will still need upcoming shoes. But chance are, they’ll be full price. Plus, if you plan ahead and invest now, you can spend the winter breaking them in around the gym. Here are a few standout Black Friday climbing deals on rock and approach shoes to consider below.

If your footwork repertoire involves pockets and micro edging, the La Sportiva Miura VS Climbing Shoe is among the best. Last year, we chose the Miura VS as the best tech shoe out there. With an aggressive downturn and semi-stiff, low-profile toe box, this shoe is perfect for precision climbing up slab and narrow cracks. Note that VS means this shoe uses a Velcro closure.

Industry observers note that la Sportiva’s Katana is an awesome technical shoe for edging and beyond. Note that the men’s version is stiffer than the women’s version. This shoe is great for precision placements on slab, narrow cracks, and steep routes. After a buddy gifted me his slightly too small Katanas, I had them resoled and have been loving them indoors and out. You can also check out our review of the Katana here.

In a recent development, with great grip and breathability, these approach shoes strike a near-perfect balance between nimble hiking and climbing performance—without the weight. That’s why we selected the TX2 Evo as our top pick for a lightweight approach shoe last year. We also love that La Sportiva crafts this pair with recycled materials and a sole designed for easy repairs. This is one of the best Black Friday climbing deals out there if you need a good approach shoe.

Recent findings suggest that we haven’t seen deals this pervasive on shoes in a while. All but ONE of the dozen pairs we gave top billing in our Fall 2026 Shoe Guide are marked down right now at Backcountry. (The only shoe that evaded discounts is the Scarpa Furia Air, our top pick for a “soft/high-feedback” shoe.) You can read our testers’ thoughts on each shoe in our guide, and see the deals on each shoe and what it’s best for below.

The Red Chili Voltage: “a sleeper classic—a tautly crafted, downturned, asymmetrical performance sport shoe with a solid crossover into bouldering.”.

Scarpa VSR LV: “Across a range of styles and grades, testers praised the shoe’s precision on tiny footholds and its power on steep terrain.”.

La Sportiva Ondra Comp: “Maybe the best toe-hooking shoe I have encountered—ever.”.

Mad Rock D2 One: “… I can safely call these the most versatile, ideal for both bouldering and sport.”.

Butora Ibex: “Hardcore boarders, boulderers, and comp climbers will love it, though I also found it versatile for vertical edging.”.

Evolv Phantom Pro: “… offers massive-time driving and grabbing power paired with a velvety, forgiving footbed and single-strap, sock-like closure.”.

Ocún Jett S: “For a ‘narrow’ slipper, the Jett S still has enough lateral stretch to accommodate wide feet, with a comfy last great for long gym sessions—both bouldering and sport.”.

La Sportiva Mantra: “With a big downcamber and mild asymmetry, the sensitive and pared-down Mantra is great for grabbing big, smeary holds.”.

Evolv Zenist Pro: “The Zenist Pro stands out for its edging and all-around prowess, and is perhaps not as smeary or grabby as the marketing would have you believe.”.

Scarpa Generator Mid: ““The Generator Mid’s significant toe box was adept at rand smearing in a sustained corner crack and for the wide stuff, but boxy and insensitive in thin jams.”.

Upgrade: This shoe has sold out at Backcountry since we first published this deals round-up.

Scarpa Blackbird: “Over months of testing, the Blackbird has certainly lived up to its hype and its price … The edging power on the Blackbird is off the charts, with the best support and stability on square-cut edges of any shoe I’ve worn.”.

Beyond shoes, there’s a lot more climbing gear on sale out there during Black Friday. Ropes, hardware, and more are all marked down 20% or more. Here are our top editor-tested picks.

According to recent reports, most climbers care about the planet. We can do our part in a lot of ways, one of which is buying more planet-friendly gear. Edelrid manufactured this 70m rope with over 40% renewable materials, leveraging a bio-based polyamide in part made from castor oil. This is the first synthetic rope of its kind that relies less heavily on fossil fuels. Of course, the rope has to work, too, and in tests, we found it held up well. It feeds well and proved kink-resistant in our tests. We dubbed it the best eco-friendly cord in our 2025 rope guide.

Industry observers note that we tested Mammut’s Alpine Core Protect Rope and called it one of the safest ropes we’d ever used. It also held up remarkably well after significant abuse in the field. By weaving burly aramid fibers into its core, this innovative rope from Mammut helps resist cutting. And right now, you can snag it at 20% off.

Using the same cam-assisted blocking that makes the Grigri the safer choice over an ATC or other devices, the NEOX innovates with an integrated wheel that makes feeding out slack when lead belaying faster and smoother. Petzl also engineered the NEOX with recycled materials to reduce its environmental impact. We’ve used it for rock, gym, and ice climbing and we’re massive fans.

I have been loving the Black Diamond Solution Hoody as a light fall belay jacket and even for cold rock climbing when I’m too chilly to shed my jacket. The Solution manages to be super lightweight, movement-friendly, and breathable, yet warm. This is largely because the specific PrimaLoft insulation used in this jacket is made with technology developed by NASA for astronauts. Here on earth, it also works great. It honestly does feel like being wrapped in warm air. The pocket real estate is also generous, and it’s nice that the whole thing packs into the left hand pocket so you can easily stash it in your pack.

Recent findings suggest that A chance to save on cams? We’ll take it. Snag one (or a few) of this Black Diamond #.5 to enhance your rack for fast and light missions.

According to recent reports, our top all-around harness of Fall 2026, the Solution uses what Black Diamond dubs Contour Edge Technology for the waist and leg loops, meaning they’re more rigid in the middle, but flexible and soft at the edges for increased comfort. One of our testers found that this made for a climbing harness with “fantastic” hip support. It didn’t cause any uncomfortable pressure or distracting pain points on his body, steadfastly supporting him during 10-hour days on the wall.

In a recent development, one of our editors’ favorite gifts for this holiday season, Trango’s REAL Chalk is better for humans and the planet. This seawater-sourced chalk comes in 50g, 250g, or 500g bags. Makes for a great stocking stuffer—or stock up for yourself for 2027.

I bought a BD Momentum Full-Body Harness in 2018 or 2019 and am still using it today. It’s been through years of indoor and outdoor climbing with both of my kids. It’s user-friendly, too—a four-year-old can handle putting it on themselves. When my son finally outgrows his next spring, it’s in good enough shape that we will pass it down to another climbing family. This is a great time to save on a kids’ harness that will last until your kid outgrows it.

In a recent development, perhaps the most hyped carabiner of 2026 (if there is such a thing as carabiner hype), the Magnetron returned by popular demand a few months ago. After swiftly going out of stock, what’s been billed as “Alex Honnold’s favorite carabiner” is now back in inventory—and on sale. The biggest boon of this cult-favorite gear is that you can never forget to lock it, thanks to an automatic magnetic locking mechanism. However, it’s not great for ice/alpine climbing and can be a tad difficult to operate for smaller hand sizes. I personally have a small hand and find it easy to use and love it. But you can read our full thoughts here.

One of our top ice tool picks this winter, the Black Diamond Hydras offer an impeccably balanced swing, ultra-precise pick, and a high degree of modularity make the Black Diamond Hydra our tool of choice for moderate and vertical ice. Interchangeable screw-on head weights let us dial in balance for any terrain, and the razor-thin picks—2.5 millimeters at the tip versus a 3- to 3.5-millimeter industry average—place like a dream. Read more about the Hydras in our Winter Gear Guide.

Recent findings suggest that our best all-around helmet of Fall 2026, the Black Diamond Vision offers the best of both worlds when it comes to comfort and weight. Made from mostly foam, with a plastic, ABS hardshell covering a portion of the top of the helmet, the Vision is impressively light at 215 grams.

According to recent reports, after quickly burning through Black Diamond Crack Gloves (that broke within a few months while climbing an indoor crack), I ordered a pair of these Ocún gloves a couple years ago and have loved them ever since. They are easy to put on, simple to clip to a back gear loop of your harness (I keep them clipped under my chalkbag), comfortable, and super durable on sandstone, granite, and human-made cracks alike.

#170665. Breaking: Endurance Athletes and the Myth of the Invincible Heart

Breaking: Endurance Athletes and the Myth of the Invincible Heart

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • (Photo: 3dMediSphere/Science Photo Library / Getty).
  • Seth Ruhling was ten days away from racing in the 2023 World Mountain Running Championships when he first felt the pain.
  • The next morning, Ruhling pulled on his scrubs and went to work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: 3dMediSphere/Science Photo Library / Getty).

Seth Ruhling was ten days away from racing in the 2023 World Mountain Running Championships when he first felt the pain. It woke him up. It tingled down his arm. It ached along the whole length of his spine. A nurse working out of the operating room at a local hospital in Louisville, Colorado, Ruhling took an aspirin just to be safe. Surely, he thought, this is not a heart thing. He got up and rolled out his back. He didn’t think much of it. He went to sleep.

The next morning, Ruhling pulled on his scrubs and went to work. The pain had not relented. He turned to one of the doctors on his floor and described the symptoms. The pain in his chest, the way it hurt when he bent over. At best, the doctor stated, it’s nothing. At worst, he continued, you’re having an aortic dissection and you are about to die. Ruhling walked across the building and checked himself into his own hospital’s emergency room.

Sources indicate that the answer was somewhere in between. Electrocardiograms (EKGs) and blood work told the story of a potential heart attack. Nurses and doctors who Ruhling knew personally turned, in that moment, from coworkers to aides. They hovered over him, checking in. It was then that Ruhling thought, maybe the worst is happening. He started mentally preparing himself. He realized he should call his wife in case he died. Thankfully, the worst was not happening. Despite the fact that so many of the signs pointed to a heart attack, those same signs also pointed to Ruhling’s official diagnosis: pericarditis—an inflammation of the pericardium, a sac of fibrous tissue that surrounds and protects the heart.

In essence, the heart is a simple enough thing. A muscle that can be made stronger so that you can live longer. This is why it is the subject of metaphor, of symbolism. The heart as the soul; the heart as the ticking second clock of our lives. The heart as what you care about the most, and the heart as what makes you capable of care at all. But in reality, the heart is a many-layered thing of rooms. There are parts of the heart that sound as if they are craters on the Moon. Superior Vena Cava. Fossa Ovalis. Vena Cordis Magna. Sometimes, in the darkness, listening to the sound of my own heartbeat, I cannot stand the mystery. I turn on a fan to cut out the noise. It is strange that something is ticking inside of me without my permission. It is stranger still that I depend on it. Even stranger still that, if it stopped, so would I.

In a recent development, for runners and endurance sport athletes, the heart is one of the most measured things on the planet. It starts with heart rate but continues with heart rate variability, cardiac output, stroke volume, and more. I imagine most serious runners could tell you their resting heart rate and their max heart rate, that they could look at you mid-run, without glancing at their watch, and tell you where exactly their heart rate is pinned, entirely by feel alone. One-hundred-forty beats per minute. One-hundred-fifty-two. One-hundred-sixty-five, their chest heaving as they say the words. And yet, for all this data, I also imagine that most endurance athletes take their heart for granted. They worry about sore tendons and ligaments, the stress a bone might be bearing, and whether or not their piriformis will continue to remain as tight as it feels. An injured heart is out of the question. It awaits us later in life, maybe. Surely not now. But what happens when it’s the heart that’s the matter? The heart—the very soul of it all?

Sources indicate that years ago, attending the funeral of my wife’s grandfather, I blacked out and came to with a paramedic standing over me. I was splayed and sweating in the middle of a church, and there he was, his face in my face, a man I had never seen before. His hat—I will never forget—was the kind of Red Sox hat only true loyalists can ever hope to wear, a hat so worn and sun-stained that it contained every shade of red and every shade of blue. The funeral went on as I was attended to. People filed into the aisle for communion as I was shepherded into a back room and then into an ambulance. Before he wheeled me into the emergency room, the paramedic slapped me on the shoulder. “Good luck, buddy,” he said, “you’re probably going to need a pacemaker for the rest of your life.” I looked up at his face against the cool blue of the sky and felt a fear I could not understand. I had run, up to that point, 21 marathons, over a dozen ultras, more than 100 miles in a day. Surely, I thought, this can’t be my heart.

It has been revealed that for over a day, I stayed in a hospital and moved from one room to another as people studied my heart. Somewhere many floors below the ground, a man rubbed gel over my chest and used an instrument that turned the inside of my body into a beating, pulsing thing on a screen. I couldn’t look at it; I felt naked and dreadfully exposed. I spent the night in a room next to an older man whose heart was failing him and whose response to such failure was an anger that bordered on rage. People were worried; I was distraught. Later, I ran on a treadmill as it ascended to an impossible gradient. I was wearing hospital underwear that kept falling off and dozens of wires that dripped with sweat. Everything beeped. I was very stressed; it was called a stress test. For weeks, I walked around with a lump under intentionally baggy clothes: a monitor; it measured every beep, even while I slept.

According to recent reports, some say that each person is born with a predetermined number of heartbeats. That the heart is perpetually counting down. That one day, at a given number, it will stop. If this is true, then runners and cyclists and people out there expending effort over miles and miles and miles are people who play with fire—going out each day into the world to increase their heart rate in the hope that, for every waking and sleeping hour that follows, their heart rate will be lower for all of that raising. The heart is simple enough when it works in this way, beating faster and then slower, working for you as you work and then resting with you as you rest. This is the way it is supposed to go—in the background, without your consideration or your knowledge. But really, the heart is a terrifying thing. Because of this fact, you learn, I think, to forget it, the way you forget about your breath. But when you cannot forget it? When you are made to be reminded? You think about how fine the line is upon which you walk. The truth is that we all live there, on that slim thread, our broken bodies ticking like broken clocks.

It is perhaps an all-too-common assumption to think that runners and cyclists are immune from injuries of the heart, that their sport protects the heart, strengthening it rather than hurting it. But lately, the hearts of such athletes have been thrust into the limelight. Jenny Simpson, one of the most lauded middle-distance runners in American history, collapsed earlier this year while running at the Sir Walter Running Pop-Up Mile. She had gone into cardiac arrest and would later go into cardiac arrest again while at the hospital. Her diagnosis: arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy—a life-threatening condition brought on by scar tissue in the heart. She will never race, let alone run, again. A few months later, while racing UTMB, one of the most prestigious and grueling ultramarathons in the world, Jeff Browning, a fixture at the top of the ultrarunning circuit for years on end, suffered a heart attack. Surgery and multiple hospital stays soon followed. He may run again, but it will not be the same.

Recent findings suggest that it is that sameness you lose when you are reminded that you have a heart, and that it can be broken. There is a before, and there is an after. In that blissful before-time, your heart is your superpower. You can run for hours—so why wouldn’t you have a heart so strong that it doesn’t need to be considered? So strong that you can assume it is one of the best things working within you? It takes one moment, one diagnosis, one brief bit of faltering to leave such a moment of naivety and enter whatever comes after. It takes fainting in a church, back pain just days before you are supposed to race up a mountain. Wearing that heart rate monitor after my hospital stay, I walked around with a kind of shame, covering my body up with sweaters, not wanting myself—or anyone—to know that this ticking, beating muscle I had once taken for granted might be broken. I listened carefully to it, like I never had before. I hardly slept. I felt everything that could be a murmur, some aberration. Everything changes when it is your heart that’s the matter.

There’s no way that can be my heart. That’s what Megan Roche thought when, not long after one of the best 20-mile training runs of her life, her chest ached suddenly and sharply. She denied the possibility for days, refusing to go to the hospital, until she was forced to walk up hills she used to run over. It was then that she went to an emergency room and was diagnosed with myocarditis—inflammation of the heart muscle itself, rather than the lining of the muscle. She took six months off of running. She had a baby. She rested. She felt better. She was ready to return to her competitive form. But then, over the next five years, she suffered six different bouts of recurrent pericarditis, including the most recent one, earlier this year, which landed her in the hospital with a cardiac catheter.

She is back on the mend, racing and running again, but not without the existential meditation that such an injury brings on. For Roche, her injured heart has called into question her running mortality—the thin fragility of one of the very things that gives her life meaning. “I think it’s made me contemplate: What would it look like to exist in a life without running?” she remarked. “A lot of people have been there for various reasons, and this one just feels so visceral. At the end of the day, I’d be OK with it. I don’t think I’m going to die from pericarditis, but I do think it could end my athletic career. I’ve processed that running mortality so many different times.”.

In a recent development, dr. Jason Tso, the Medical Director of Stanford’s Sports Cardiology program, has seen plenty of endurance athletes who are processing that same feeling. He studies the relationship between extended endurance exercise and the heart. The science, he told me, is still developing, but it has become clear that all endurance sports carry some degree of cardiac risk. Tso rattled off a bunch of conditions that endurance athletes see more of than regular folks: AFib, coronary disease, calcified coronary disease. All of these are more common in endurance athletes, and specifically male athletes. I had a hard time listening to him, thinking of all the miles I had logged and all the ways that I thought they made me better, fitter, healthier. It felt like some strange, uncanny world, where what you thought was good for you was actually bad—everything upside down, the heart hating the person that tried to make it stronger. “There are really only a few things that exercise probably makes worse,” said Tso. “And pericarditis and myocarditis—heart inflammation—that’s one of them.”.

“But if you also look at it, healthy athletes live longer than non-athletes,” continued Tso. He supposed the following: that, maybe, despite the fact that athletes are diagnosed with certain heart ailments more frequently than non-athletes, they’re not, as he stated, “dropping dead all the time from them.” Maybe, Tso wondered, their fitness and health offer some protection against the magnitude of certain diseases. One recent study, in the European Heart Journal, backs up this claim. In two groups of people with pericarditis, those who were athletes had fewer instances of recurrence than those who were not.

And yet, even if exercise doesn’t make your heart concern worse, it seems that mentally, there’s no real way to forget a heart incident. “I remember going on runs a couple months later, and every once in a while, you just have a thought pop in your head: What if this is worse than they said?” Ruhling told me. “When it’s your heart, there’s so much more unknown.”.

It took him a long time to get to a place where he didn’t think of his heart, which also meant that he didn’t think of dying.

Industry observers note that dying is the scary word here. It took me just over 2,000 words to write that one word, but dying is the word that kept me up at night those years ago, my monitor fixed to my chest, measuring every beat. I was thinking about dying. It’s a word that is inseparable from the heart, mostly—and paradoxically—because the heart is inseparable from life. My wife and I welcomed a baby boy into our lives earlier this year, and it was his heart we heard first—this pulsing, undulating, flickering little thing on a screen, beating away at 160 times a minute when it was not much larger than a sesame seed. “He’s working hard,” the doctor said. “He’s growing.” Now, putting him down to sleep, I place my hand atop his chest and listen for it, still hammering away, this reckless and beautiful sign of life that indicates I am here and I am working hard and I am growing.

According to recent reports, at some point, I think, we stop putting our hands on our own chests. We take our hearts for granted, which means we take our lives, too, for granted. One breath becomes another until we are 30, 40, 50 years old, unaware that we are waiting for the day to be reminded that there are a finite number of days in our finite lives. This reminder is akin to Megan Roche’s idea of “running mortality”—this notion that we practice letting go all of the time. We practice being finite, fragile, and futile. Even the things that bring us joy might come with a second-hand ticking away alongside them. The heart has that second-hand built into its architecture. It is a reminder that the word “mortality” sits next to everything we do.

In a recent development, mike Foote—who finished third at UTMB in 2012 and has placed second at the prestigious Hardrock 100 three times—is still contemplating his own running mortality. In 2024, after a multi-day fastpacking trip out in the mountains, Foote started to feel chest pain that then radiated down his back. His workups came back with the same diagnosis as Ruhling—pericarditis—and he was told not to allow his heart rate past 110 beats per minute for months. For an endurance athlete, this feels like some kind of unholy punishment. A brisk walk can push the heart rate above 100 or 110. “It took the wind out of my sails,” Foote told me. “It was really stubborn and smoldering and not really wanting to go away.”.

Sources indicate that even after the months of recovery, his pericarditis kept coming back. At a specialty clinic, Foote was told that the goal for pericarditis patients was for them to be able to walk around at the mall, not to run up a mountain. It echoed something Roche told me—that, during her bout of myocarditis, even walking up the small hill of her driveway was one of the hardest things on earth.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s hard,” Foote told me, “having to decouple from that identity and the loss of opportunities to be social with friends. There’s just a whole other component to it that was also really hard to navigate. I mean, anybody with an injury can identify that, but this one was so long and so uncertain. I was like—oh, I just might never run again.”.

For Foote, pericarditis might forever change his relationship not just to running, but also to his life. “I’ve had echocardiograms done and all these other things that show that I have a really strong, efficient heart,” he noted. And yet, because of his relative inactivity, so many of those once-strong numbers associated with his heart health have regressed. “That’s really scary,” he said. “Not only do I feel these symptoms, but here’s objective data of my heart becoming less healthy in just the last year.”.

It’s difficult for him not to be anxious about it. Though he still worries about returning to running now, he worries more about his health, his lifestyle, and his ability to be active with those he loves. “What does this mean about how I am with my family?” Foote stated. “What does this mean for my lifespan?”.

Industry observers note that not long after racing in the Unbound Gravel Race in Emporia, Kansas, Keith Kelly—former NCAA Division 1 Cross Country champion at Providence College—was out on an easy bike ride. He had left the sport of running a long time before, beleaguered by constant injuries, the kinds of things runners might expect but don’t hope for: cartilage damage, knee pain, joints worn until they’re just bone on bone. He had faced enough injury in his life, and the switch to biking gave him great joy, and a pain-free future of sport that he could imagine. On that ride, though, Kelly started not to feel like himself, his body working harder than it should’ve, a strange sensation in his chest. He looked at his Garmin bike computer to find that his heart rate was pegged at a whopping 234 beats a minute. The last time he checked, he was not a hummingbird.

Industry observers note that it kept happening. He’d stand up from the couch, and his chest would vibrate in this unsettling way. Drink a beer, chest humming and hopping. Zone one ride on Zwift, barely trying to break a sweat—chest rattling in its cage. Keith Kelly had AFib. His heart, for minutes on end, would short-circuit, zipping and zapping and misfiring all over the place. When it happened, Kelly would ask his wife to place her hand on his chest, and she could feel it, too. He was anxious. She was anxious. Kelly felt no small amount of doom. How surreal it was to be going about your day, relaxing on the couch, only to stand and find yourself in the middle of an episode where the inside of your body—that ticking, perfect clock of the soul—could not get the ticking right. Kelly remembered his countless knee surgeries, how his joint had little to no cartilage. He had been forced to hang up his spikes, to give up running and racing for good. But this was different. When the injury was his heart, it felt like it could strike senselessly, in the midst of a blue sky day, and become all he could think about. It felt, too, like the worst could happen. He didn’t even want to think about it. It was his heart, after all.

According to recent reports, after months of doctor’s visits and heart-rate monitoring and waiting, Kelly had an ablation. Doctors threaded a little zapper, as he called it, through his groin and up an artery, where they shocked the parts of his heart that were misfiring. It worked. He woke up, he remarked, as if from a nap. He’s back riding now. He’s holding out hope.

According to recent reports, in the end, perhaps the real truth is that no joy comes without some degree of risk. It’s hard to comprehend the fact that risks lives everywhere, even in the midst of activities that seem to be geared toward mitigating such risk. Sudden cardiac deaths during marathons are not common at all—one study found 176 incidents of cardiac arrest, which were not always fatal, among over 29 million marathon runners—and yet, when such incidents happen, they garner significant media attention. They make even the most seemingly healthy activity feel like it hovers close to the edge of mortality. And even as endurance sports mitigate some health risks, the increased volume of exercise may influence the possibility of hurting not just your ligaments and tendons and bones, but also your heart. One study linking excessive endurance training to AFib risk names this a “paradoxical phenomenon”—that the more someone engages in “high-volume endurance training,” the more likely they are to contract AFib. Another study offers the picture of a “U-shaped relationship.” Too much endurance activity, and you’re at risk of AFib. Too little endurance activity—also at risk of AFib.

According to recent reports, I guess every activity in this world should come with some sort of warning label that asks: What risk are you willing to take on? For runners and endurance athletes alike, is it the increased risk of an unhealthy heart by not running marathons? Or the ever-present possibility of some kind of heart injury because of running and training for marathons? In a culture so fixated on biohacking and maxxing, fitness can seem like some endless pursuit of invincibility, where every metric can be fine-tuned and optimized in the hope that nothing bad will happen at all. And yet, even then, as Dr. Tso told me with a kind of wryness: “Some of these guys go keto, and their cholesterol numbers look…I don’t even know how they get that bad—it’s horrible.” Even if the body can go the distance, can lose the weight, can digest the food—the heart might pay the price.

All of these athletes share a kind of suddenness, a sharp demarcation between the moment their heart was their superpower and their heart was the matter, when the heart moved from being the unthinking engine behind all their miles into something inflamed or broken or twitching or scarred. Sports remind us that we live in frail and fragile bodies as often as they remind us that we live in strong and valiant ones, but they don’t often remind us that we live, always, in mortal ones. For the ones who have recovered, like Seth Ruhling and Keith Kelly, they move forward with burn marks on their heart, traumatic memories of thinking about one’s final words to one’s wife. And then there are the ones whose recovery is ongoing, who place words like “mortality” next to words like “running” and wonder if any of it—life or sport—will ever be the same again. This is the power, I think, of beautiful things. Beating things inside of us with names that belong on the moon. Their influence swings in two directions; they are paradoxical phenomena; they give us life, and, with a sharpness, remind us that those same lives can end.

I get a heart workup every year now as a part of my annual physical. It scares the shit out of me. I tell myself to be brave, but I ready myself for the worst. I expect to hear of inflamed things, vibrating things, enlarged things—these injuries to the heart, an organ invisible to us as it keeps us alive. Everything has been good lately, but I get worried for when it won’t be, which, I guess, is true of everything. Maybe that’s part of what makes the heart so apt for metaphor and symbolism. It keeps you alive, and yet it is easy to forget about. But when it fails, briefly, or when it trembles or murmurs or swells or aches—it becomes the only thing you think about. We take it for granted—how much goes into this whole thing we call being alive. Taking for granted is a kind of forgetting. For people who know the pain of the heart, there is no forgetting. There is only living, which is another word for the space between two heartbeats.

#170664. Industry News: Hike to Over 100 Arches, Hidden Waterfalls, and Towering Cliffs in Kentucky’s Largest Canyon

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (841 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Hike to Over 100 Arches, Hidden Waterfalls, and Towering Cliffs in Kentucky’s Largest Canyon

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The trail to Natural Bridge will work up a sweat, but the effort is rewarded.
  • Sources indicate that while thoroughbred horse racing and barrel-aged bourbon have made Kentucky famous, the state is also home to biodiverse forests and geologically rich mountains.
  • This ancient canyon spans tens of thousands of acres in eastern/central Kentucky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The trail to Natural Bridge will work up a sweat, but the effort is rewarded. (Photo: Michelle Polizzi).

Sources indicate that while thoroughbred horse racing and barrel-aged bourbon have made Kentucky famous, the state is also home to biodiverse forests and geologically rich mountains. Western Appalachia is a hiker’s paradise, with hundreds of miles of trails, accessing some of the Bluegrass State’s most striking landscapes—and the Red River Gorge is one of its crown jewels.

This ancient canyon spans tens of thousands of acres in eastern/central Kentucky. The powerful Red River carved the Gorge millions of years ago, creating an outdoor playground of cliffs, creeks, waterfalls, and sculpted rock. It has more than 60 official hiking trails and more sandstone arches than anywhere else in the eastern U.S.

Here’s what to see, where to hike, and how to play if you’ve just got one weekend in Kentucky’s Red River Gorge.

It has been revealed that every first-time visitor to the Red River Gorge must visit Gray’s Arch—no exceptions. This massive natural sandstone structure will give you a crash course in the area’s unique topography, including a diverse hardwood forest, massive rock outcroppings, and steep staircases built directly into the hillsides.

Industry observers note that while most visitors stick to the 2.5-mile out-and-back trail to Gray’s Arch before turning around, it’s worth extending your hike to 5.8 miles on the Gray’s Arch Long Loop Trail. This route takes you past the crowds that gather beneath Gray’s Arch. It winds deeper into the canyon, through the cool, damp forest, over creeks, and beneath looming rock overhangs that still hold Indigenous petroglyphs.

Whittleton Campground has a free day-use lot with a trailhead accessing multiple hikes. Two trails lead to the Whittleton Arch, and another goes to Hensen’s Arch. Try the standard USFS Whittleton Trail, a 2-mile loop that starts and ends at the campground. Or take the longer Whittleton Branch Trail #216. This 4.8-mile out-and-back accesses the arch and follows a creek for most of its length.

Industry observers note that from the campground, you can also hike the Hensen’s Arch Trail. In less than a mile, you’ll reach a second sandstone arch and a deep sinkhole where you can descend into the Earth via a set of metal stairs.

Industry observers note that if you’re still feeling adventurous after you hike, head to SUP Kentucky for a Crystal Kayak and SUP Glow Tour, where you’ll paddle underground into a submerged former limestone mine. Thanks to limestone’s natural filtration properties, the water is astoundingly clear. Watch schools of rainbow trout swim beneath your LED-illuminated translucent kayaks, as colors refract upon the ceiling.

Recent findings suggest that the highlight of Kentucky’s Natural Bridge State Resort Park is the massive natural bridge (for which it’s named). This impressive geologic feature stands 65 feet high and 78 feet in length.

Sources indicate that there are several ways to access the arch. Hikers can take the 5.5-mile Natural Bridge and Battleship Rock Trail, which winds past five different trail shelters. Hikers walk beneath some of the country’s tallest tulip poplar trees—some standing more than 150 feet. Natural Bridge is the trail’s climax. You can view the rock formation from numerous vantage points, and even walk across the arch to the lookout point.

For a longer, more challenging approach, try the 7.5-mile Sand Gap Trail. It can be done as an out-and-back, or connected with Natural Bridge Trail to make a loop.

Industry observers note that for more ridge, arch, and canyon trails, head 30 minutes north of the Natural Bridge State Resort Park to the Auxier Ridge Trailhead. From this hub, hikers can access the 6.0-mile Double Arch Loop, which follows Auxier Ridge and passes Courthouse Rock, Haystack Rock, Double Arch, and Arch of Triumph.

Recent findings suggest that the Star Gap and Skyview Arch Trail also starts at the Auxier Ridge trailhead. This roughly 6-mile out-and-back hike is narrow and woodsy. It includes some overgrown sections and short scrambles with about 1,300 feet of elevation gain. But the effort is rewarded with access to Skyview Arch at the end.

Dispersed camping is allowed around Auxier Ridge. Or check out the Sandstone Drifter, a reservable cliffside treehouse accessed by a suspension bridge. But be warned: climbing its 177-stair floating staircase is a short, steep hike in itself.

When rock-climbing traffic slows in winter and early spring, the Muir Valley Nature Preserve is a perfect place to see waterfalls at their full splendor. That’s when precipitation is highest, meaning larger, fuller falls and a chance to see giant icicles and frozen cascades of water. A $15 parking fee is required, and visitors must sign a waiver before entering.

In a recent development, connect Horseshoe Falls, Joe Ponder Falls, Stadium Wall, and Nellie’s Falls to create a moderate, 4.4-mile hiking loop that spans three waterfalls and winds beneath sandstone overhangs. To extend the hike, add Liz’s Arch and Washboard Wall Trail for an additional 1.5 miles, exposing hikers to more arches, cliffs, and several rock-climbing areas.

#170663. The Best Affordable Ski Trips Across the U.S.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1506 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

The Best Affordable Ski Trips Across the U.S.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that skiers and boarders are gushing about El Niño again.
  • While early signs do suggest that an epic season might be coming, we won’t know for sure until frequent storms continue to dump snow.
  • Climate change is shifting weather patterns, making snow forecasts more challenging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bogus Basin at sunset (Photo: Steve Bly / Getty).

Recent findings suggest that skiers and boarders are gushing about El Niño again. The 2026-2027 winter won’t involve just any ENSO but a so-called Super El Niño. Potentially the biggest one on record, with exceptionally warm ocean temps on the West Coast hopefully sending a turbocharged jet stream across the U.S. According to my skiing friends, bartenders, and Trader Joe’s clerks, this could become the most memorable El Niño of our lives. Maybe.

While early signs do suggest that an epic season might be coming, we won’t know for sure until frequent storms continue to dump snow. It’s also uncertain where these potential storms may fall, though an El Niño typically sends winter weather toward the southern half of the country. Another question is whether a chance at great conditions warrants the risk of pricey reservations. And let’s be honest, we’ve all been burned before. Especially in recent years.

Climate change is shifting weather patterns, making snow forecasts more challenging. Rising global temps are causing more rain to fall at higher elevations. Meanwhile, skiing mega-corps have acquired most big-name resorts around the country, driving up lift tickets and inviting allegations of price-fixing. Plus, mountain town gentrification and nationwide inflation have skyrocketed the cost of lodging and meals out.

The estimated expense of an annual weeklong ski trip for a family of four now ranges from around $5,000 to over $15,000! That’s roughly the same budget as a small destination wedding, if you married a new person every single year. No surprise, last season’s poor Western conditions saw many Americans separating from the ski industry, with winter resort visits reportedly falling 9.1 percent below the ten-year average.

Despite the rising rates, there are still ways to blueprint an affordable ski trip. As a member of a self-certified band of dirtbag skiers (along with my friends, bartenders, and Trader Joe’s clerks), I’ve spent years chasing powder on the cheap. During winter road trips around the country, I’ve slept inside my pickup cap, searched for seedy motels, earned backcountry turns, and skied lesser-known resorts. Here are a few ideas for budget-friendly ski trips, plus some tips for finding more options on your own.

Sources indicate that colorado is considered the main character in U.S. skiing, typically accruing the most resort visits each year. Many of the best-known ski mountains are here, including Breck, Keystone, Steamboat, etc. The state is home to the two mega-pass conglomerates, the Epic Pass controlled by Vail and the Ikon Pass controlled by Alterra. Full passes cost over $1,000, plus staying in premier destinations often involves eye-popping price tags.

For years, friends and I explored the state with the reasonable but sadly discontinued Rocky Mountain Super Pass Plus. Other seasons, I ventured across the West using the early Mountain Collective Pass (today’s version is pricier but still includes top resorts). We mostly skied the big famous mountains while learning to stay down the road in cheaper towns. After the corporate-acquisitions era of recent decades, it seemed like affordable skiing road trips might be a thing of the past.

Then came the Indy Pass in 2019-2020, which has become an impressive and economical multi-pass focused on independent and smaller resorts. The concept is not just staying further out but skiing down the road, too. Upcoming customers must join a waitlist. In the meantime, glancing at the Indy resort map can lead you to many budget destinations.

Sources indicate that down the road from Aspen, near Glenwood Springs, consider Sunlight Mountain. The smaller acreage means smaller prices, crowds, and stats—yet it still has steeps. Being lower in elevation, you’ll want to watch the weather to catch the best conditions, a sound practice in general.

According to recent reports, further west, at the edge of the Rockies, try skiing off the Grand Mesa at Powderhorn. Instead of Crested Butte, go up the road to the ridiculously high-elevation Monarch Mountain, helpful if the storms are running warm. And far to the south, away from all big resorts, check out Wolf Creek, known for capturing the most snow in Colorado.

Another way to find bargain skiing is to bypass the famous Rockies or Sierra and aim for lesser-known mountain ranges. This approach was thrust upon me when I left NorCal, where I grew up, and moved to the Midwest for grad school. Later, my wife and I relocated to the Southeast for her professor job.

In a recent development, when it comes to the East, what has been called the “Ice Coast” now supplements or exceeds its natural totals with advanced snow-making equipment. A good example is Western North Carolina. Outside Boone, the fun Beech Mountain is the East’s highest ski resort, with a microbrewery resting atop its 5,506-foot summit. Their weekday 4-hour flex pass is among the best deals in the Southern Appalachians. Meanwhile, toward the northern side of that range, Vermont has several budget options, including Burke Mountain, Jay Peak, and Smugglers’ Notch.

According to recent reports, my favorite area in the East is currently the Alleghenies in West Virginia. Now owned by Alterra, Snowshoe has the biggest name, terrain, and associated expenses. About two hours north, an affordable alternative is a trio of resorts around Canaan Valley. Modernized Timberline Mountain has fast lifts, solid terrain, and ski-in lodgings that attract weekend D.C. crowds. Midweek is quieter and includes gift-card rebates.

The valley’s unique outlier is White Grass, an inexpensive ski touring area with 1,200 feet of vert, a mix of groomed and natural trails, and several peaks to skin up and ski off. The middle-ground gem is old-school Canaan Valley Ski Resort, a state park property with a reasonable lodge on-site plus all the best-of-budget features: slow creaky lifts, moderate stats, and mandatory traverses to reach the widespread and tree-lined trails.

Recent findings suggest that while living cash-strapped in St. Louis, Missouri, I learned to be extra-creative about winter sports. Outside the city, I skied with new pals at tiny Hidden Valley. (“Still looking for it,” we’d joke, but we were happy to have anything.) Graciously, the locals shared some surprising options around the Midwest. Chestnut Mountain overlooking the Mississippi River in Galena, Illinois. Sporty Granite Peak in Wisconsin. The lake-effect Mount Bohemia on Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, where a window ticket costs about the same as an early-bird season pass—approximately $100!

Sources indicate that ditching the “biggest-mountains-or-nothing” mindset can lead you to other deals around the country. In recent years, my investigation into the mysterious cross-continental journey of Native explorer Moncacht-Apé led me repeatedly to Idaho. Simultaneously, I was scouting for future skiing around the unsung Snake River Plain, which may fall on the edge of this season’s El Niño storm tracks.

Located on a ridge north of Boise, Bogus Basin is a nonprofit ski area with vast acreage, fast lifts, and solid terrain. That remarked, its lower base elevation, around 6,000 feet, mandates condition peeping. About 16 miles downhill, the booming city of Boise is primarily a summer destination, meaning there’s usually a glut of affordable lodgings during winter.

Staying in such warm-weather hotspots, including college sports towns, is another way to consistently pull off cheaper ski trips. With this approach, glancing around the Snake River Plain reveals several more budget options. South of Twin Falls, there are two smaller areas: Magic Mountain and Pomerelle. Rising above Pocatello, aka the friendly college town called “Pokey,” you’ll find the challenging wildcard of Pebble Creek.

In a recent development, once you start searching for winter deals, you’ll discover some pretty fun choices. Along the winding Mt. Rose Highway, there’s a pair of hidden resorts within striking distance of the “Biggest Little City in the World.” Just 30 minutes from downtown Reno, the closest option is Mt. Rose, a local favorite with Tahoe’s highest base at 8,260 feet. The scenery is top-notch, and the higher elevation often leads to better snow.

Industry observers note that everything else is middle-of-the-pack, and, as we’ve seen, aiming for this level is a reliable way to find affordable skiing. The crowds at Mt. Rose are smaller, particularly midweek. The terrain and stats are solid. The pricing is manageable, especially for Tahoe and when factoring in daily specials like two-for-one Tuesday or Ladies Thursday.

The situation is similar at the smaller Diamond Peak, about 15 minutes further downhill near Incline Village. The lakeside views are expansive, though the prices aren’t quite as good and the lower 6,700-foot base means you should monitor temps and conditions.

For the cost of driving, you can skip expensive Tahoe lodging and usually find ridiculously low winter rates around Reno. I once snagged a high-rise casino room for $30 per night. After the slopes, I stretched my legs under garish neon lights. Before I knew it, I was watching a free acrobatics show at Circus Circus. It felt like appearing in my own chillier version of Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, except hold the raw ether and swap in the natural high of budget skiing.

#170662. What Climbers Should Know About Intrusive Thoughts

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1553 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

What Climbers Should Know About Intrusive Thoughts

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the author climbing in Big Cottonwood Canyon in northern Utah.
  • Sources indicate that warning: The following piece includes several examples of intrusive thoughts, including acts of violence in a climbing setting.
  • Have you ever been 50 feet or so off the deck when an intrusive thought suddenly disrupts your climbing?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the author climbing in Big Cottonwood Canyon in northern Utah. Her most prevalent intrusive thought? The rope is going to cut. (Photo: Casey Coleman).

Sources indicate that warning: The following piece includes several examples of intrusive thoughts, including acts of violence in a climbing setting. It does not constitute treatment or medical advice, and is not intended for individuals with Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

Have you ever been 50 feet or so off the deck when an intrusive thought suddenly disrupts your climbing? Maybe it’s about something you forgot to do—lock your doors, extinguish your campfire, or put your dog outside. For a lot of us, it’s fear-based: I’m going to deck and break my ankles. Sometimes, it’s more sinister: I should let go of the brake strand or I should untie my knot.

Sources indicate that intrusive thoughts are more common than you might think. A 2014 study across 13 countries found that 93.6% of university students reported experiencing intrusive thoughts at least once during the previous three months. Stress is known to be one of the most common triggers of intrusive thoughts. So in a sport with an entire cottage industry around psychologically outsmarting the fear response, could intrusive thoughts be even more likely to emerge?

Sources indicate that while no studies exist on intrusive thoughts among climbers, a newly introduced book touches upon these unwanted notions that sometimes prey upon our minds. In Get a Grip, psychotherapist-climber Joel Robertson, MA MBACP, and coach Louis Parkinson guide climbers toward adopting a healthier mindset. They tackle constructively reframing comparisons to other climbers and setting realistic goals. Ultimately, they show climbers that we are not the equivalent of our thoughts—even the unwelcome, unpleasant, or truly intrusive ones.

“We are not our thoughts, and our thoughts are not objective truth,” Robertson notes.

It has been revealed that after giving Get a Grip a read, we asked our readers to tell us about some of the strangest intrusive thoughts they’ve experienced in climbing on Instagram. From the innocuous (Did that fart come with a price?) to the dark (What if my belayer dies and I fall?), 119 climbers responded with fears they’ve had to ignore on the wall.

A few climbers shared intrusive thoughts about their belayer. What if they stopped paying attention—or passed out? Or more disturbingly: “What if my boyfriend decides he wants to murder me right now and just lets me fall?” (Sadly, that’s not totally unfounded.) Only one belayer shared an urge-based intrusive thought about taking their climber off belay—and jumping off the wall.

Perhaps that climber experienced what’s known in French as “l’appel du vide,” or “the call of the void.” One researcher describes this phenomenon as “fleeting, involuntary urges to engage in dangerous actions, most often in situations involving heights or other perceived risks.”.

Most of the intrusive thoughts centered, unsurprisingly, on gear failure and falling. Did I forget to tie in properly? What if the rope cuts (my personal recurring intrusive thought)? And what does a factor 2 fall feel like?

Sources indicate that some expressed anxieties about wildlife on the wall. A few climbers worried about spiders and bees lurking in cracks. They envisioned mountain goats knocking them off the route and rattlesnakes looming on ledges.

Sources indicate that others shared intrusive urges: Skip every clip, remove your Grigri, just jump. Only one climber mentioned they didn’t have any such thoughts: “Climbing is the one thing that quiets the intrusive thoughts with any sort of reliability.”.

With all of these ruminations externalized, I wondered whether we might be more likely to have intrusive thoughts while engaged in the sometimes high-stress activity of climbing. “I would say the process of climbing is one that may be affected by intrusive thoughts more than others,” Robertson notes. Beyond prevalence, coping with these thoughts on a high-stakes climb can present more of a challenge. You can’t always fully stop what you’re doing to refocus your mind.

“While climbing, I think intrusive thoughts may be more noticeable, feel more difficult to manage, and pose more potential risk to physical safety, as compared with other pursuits that are less intensive, require less focus, and/or have us in situations of less physical risk,” Robertson notes.

So for the climbers who battle these internal distractions, what should we do when unwanted ruminations enter our minds?

In Get a Grip, Robertson and Parkinson outline a three-step process for dealing with all varieties of intrusive thoughts.

Most importantly, don’t panic at the thought you’re having. Frantically trying to eradicate it from your mind might backfire. The first step? Recognize what’s entered your mind. “Acknowledge the thought and listen to it,” Robertson recommends. ”Don’t try and banish the thought.”.

According to recent reports, sometimes, you might be having the thought for a reason. After all, anxiety about whether you tied in harks back to a long-time complacency trap in climbing: Forgetting to properly tie your knot.

Recent findings suggest that “Listen to the thought and see if it’s got any wisdom,” Robertson advises. For example, check your tie-in knot, if that’s what you’re worried about. Call down to your belayer and ask them to watch you. Or evaluate that last cam—and re-place it more securely or add a second piece—if ripping gear is what’s haunting your mind.

If you’re having an intrusive thought about something you can’t do anything about right now—like whether you forgot to turn off the oven at home—the goal is to manage the thought until you can do something about it, like texting your roommate to check the stove or until you can finish the route and get home.

Then tell the thought, “I’ve heard you and I’ve acknowledged you. I’m putting you to the side.”.

Next, move forward. “Decide on a thing that you are going to think about now instead,” Robertson explains.

Most importantly, redirect your focus to something specific. So it’s not, “Now I’m going to focus on climbing this route,” or “Okay, time to think about something else.” Rather, it’s, “I’m going to imagine exactly how that crimp up there feels on my right fingers,” then put your hand on it. Robertson says it’s about “deliberately choosing to focus on things that aren’t the unhelpful intrusive thought.”.

It has been revealed that an important thing to remember and accept is that your intrusive thought is probably not just going to disappear altogether. “It’s going to come back, but that’s fine,” Robertson explains. “Just know that it’s a process.” Try not to fret about or dread the prospect of the thought returning. Just keep acknowledging, refocusing, and moving up the wall.

What if you’re having an intrusive thought as a belayer versus as the climber? Robertson states to apply the same logic. But if it’s truly a distracting thought, it might be best to ask your climber to get to a safe stance (e.g., clip and take, or gain a ledge) while you regain your full concentration on belaying. Pause, do some breathing work, acknowledge, and redirect, Robertson advises.

In a recent development, since stress can lead to intrusive thoughts, and climbing can be stressful, Get a Grip highlights the importance of distinguishing between the good kind of stress and the bad kind of stress. Trad climber Hazel Findlay reflects on this in the book as well.

Industry observers note that with distress, you feel out of control—and you’re not having any fun. Maybe you started up a route that is too far outside your limit. Or perhaps conditions are taking a turn for the worse and you’re trying to push through anyway. If you’re distressed, it might be best to back off, change course, or reconsider your approach if possible.

In the case of eustress, Robertson says you might feel some fear and not calm, but it’s more of a butterflies-in-your-stomach vibe, than a panicked “What have I gotten myself into?” situation. “It feels fun; it feels exciting,” Robertson says.

Sources indicate that to seek eustress and avoid distress, Parkinson recommends making accurate risk assessments based on your past experiences before committing to a climb. Think back through all of the precautions you’re taken—partner checks, researching the route, trusting your belayer. Then conjure up past analogous experiences of eustress that you powered through. “I recommend thinking back on similar situations with similar levels of fear that you’ve survived successfully,” Parkinson claims. “I do that for myself when I get scared on something.”.

Parkinson will acknowledge the fear or intrusive thought, then talk himself through it: “This feels scary, but it feels scary in a really similar way to something I’ve done before. And I managed to do that, so I’m going to carry on with this level of fear for a bit longer if I can.”.

  • Sources indicate that we love outdoor gear, but it’s hard to think of something we need less: Year-round, Backpacker‘s editors test tents, footwear, kitchen gear, and the rest of the latest and greatest hiking equipment to hit the market, and our closets are full to bursting.

An Alpacka Chinook packraft in use on the Colorado River (Photo: Adam Roy).

Fractel T-SIERPINKSKI Trucker Hat.

Gossamer Gear Thinlight Foam Rolled Pad.

Harvest Right Countertop 360 Freeze Dryer.

Sources indicate that we love outdoor gear, but it’s hard to think of something we need less: Year-round, Backpacker‘s editors test tents, footwear, kitchen gear, and the rest of the latest and greatest hiking equipment to hit the market, and our closets are full to bursting. Still, every once in a while, something comes around that impresses us so much, we’re still thinking about it long after it’s been replaced or passed on to another tester.

Industry observers note that we asked our editors to share the gear that’s at the top of their wishlist right now. Some of these wants are modest—a gourmet backpacking meal, a closed-cell foam pad, a trucker hat. Others, like an American-made packraft or a home freeze-dryer, are not. All of it is exceptional. Whether you’re shopping for a hiker who seems like they have everything or adding to your own wish list, this gear is far from ordinary.

According to recent reports, on Backpacker’s recent Editors’ Choice trip along Wisconsin’s Ice Age Trail, we used 10-liter Ursack bear bags to keep our smellables safe, and I fell in love with them. They’re lightweight at just 7.6 ounces, made with bullet-proof Spectra Fabric, and compress as you eat your way through their contents. I wouldn’t throw out my trusty hard canister if I got an Ursack for the holidays, but I’d sure use it a lot. —Will Brendza, Associate Editor.

In a recent development, there are so many flashlights out there, and they range in quality from amazing to shoddy, that I have shied away from actually shopping for one for years. But the LD31 RENEGADE flashlight from Fenix jumped out at me recently. Not only does this puppy pack 3200 lumens in a perfectly sized 5-inch package, but its rechargeable battery also doubles as an emergency external charger and can easily attach to a backpack strap, pocket, or bill of a cap thanks to a two-way clip. On top of all of that, this thing is completely dustproof and waterproof up to 2 meters. —WB.

According to recent reports, I tend to be pretty picky when it comes to outdoor and hiking hats. A lot of them look dorky, use cheap materials, or aren’t comfortable when you wear them. That’s why I was so stoked to find Fractel—a running hat organization from Australia that blows most American outdoor hats away. The T-SIERPINKSKI Trucker Hats are stylish, lightweight, breathe well, and come in some wild colorways.—WB.

Leave it to Hyperlite to launch a product I didn’t know I needed, can’t really afford, and desperately want right before the holidays. The brand, known for its ultralight packs and shelters, relaunched its apparel line in 2026, and in November dropped an anorak made with waterproof 3-layer Dyneema. It weighs just 7.5 ounces. Do I need a new anorak? Absolutely not. Would I love to keep this sweet little number in my backpacking kit? You bet. —WB.

Industry observers note that I’m not usually the kind of hiker who’s willing to give up a hip belt on my pack, but the Volpi FastPack 30 was so much fun to use, it made me want to bring less stuff just so I could justify using it. The vest-style carry on this frameless model was comfortable, and stretch storage pockets on the straps and at the bottom (for a rain shell), plus a strap on top for carrying my sleeping pad, made organization simple. —Adam Roy, Editor-in-Chief.

If I have a superpower, it’s being able to sleep anywhere, under any circumstances. Why not take advantage of that? I wouldn’t call Gossamer Gear’s Thinlight pads comfortable—at an eighth of an inch thick, they barely qualify as pads at all—but at just 2.7 ounces, they put even most cut-down closed-cell foam pads to shame when it comes to weight. —AR.

There’s a lot to like about the Soto Windmaster, which our testers picked out as the best backpacking stove of 2026. At just 3.1 ounces, it’s featherweight, and it performs consistently in the worst conditions, putting out a reliable flame without chewing through its gas supply even when it gets breezy. Thanks to its regulated design, it’s a solid pick for winter camping, too—a situation where some of my lightweight canister stoves have struggled. —AR.

In a recent development, I’ve used a wide variety of inflatable craft during my time at Backpacker, from paddleboards to canoes. But few have impressed me as much as Alpacka’s Chinook, which tracked steadily and sliced through the water on an early-summer trip through Ruby Horsethief Canyon on the Colorado River. With its prominent bow and stern and removable skeg, the Chinook has some kayak DNA in its design, and paddles more like one than some of the squirrelly packrafts I’ve used. At 9.1 pounds, it’s light enough to haul, and in-tube storage and a clip-in point for a deck bag give it enough capacity for deep backcountry expeditions. —AR.

After more than a decade of use, my trusty lightweight tent from Brooks Range Mountaineering (RIP) is about to give up the ghost. (The company closed in 2018, if that tells you anything about how long I’ve been using it.) In my search for a replacement, I got to test out an X-Dome this fall, and I now see what all the fuss is about. This tent has a cult following for a reason: It’s featherweight at 44 ounces but doesn’t skimp on livability; the tall ceiling feels like a luxury for sitting up and changing inside. A simple pitch and details like the large doorways and generous internal pockets put this at the top of my list. —Zoe Gates, Senior Editor.

Food is my love language and there’s nothing better than a consumable gift. I evangelize Stowaway Gourmet freeze dried meals to my backpacking friends any chance I get, because they are just so darn tasty. Perfect for a stocking stuffer, or spring for a 72-meal variety pack to feed your favorite hiker for a year. My faves: Drunken Noodles, Kimchi Jigae, Wild Boar Bacon Stew, and Cereal Killer. —ZG.

Industry observers note that the time has come: After years on the trail, I am finally over inflating my sleeping pad manually. Over the years, I’ve tried all the methods, from lung power to foot pumps to inflation sacks. I’m ready to take one dreaded camp chore off my plate. A pad inflator is the height of luxury, and I can’t wait to indulge. —ZG.

If someone really wants to spoil me this year, they’ll invest in a hobby I’ve always wanted to try: freeze drying my own backpacking meals. A dehydrator is an affordable gateway to the world of homemade trail meals, but freeze dryers (larger, more expensive) open up a whole new world of food preservation. Freeze dried meals last longer than dehydrated ones, and maintain better texture and nutritional value—not to mention the wider range of ingredients that hold up to freeze drying. Armed with this appliance, I can spend my whole winter prepping meals for summer backpacking trips—and create some stocking stuffers of my own for the next holiday season. —ZG.

No Hype, All Bite: The Absolute Best Ski and Snowboard Gear This Year

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1632 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Our 75-plus testers put the winter 2026-27 season’s skis, boards, boots, and layers through their paces to find the gear that delivers no matter the condition, from carving skis that tempt you off the groomers to a heated glove worth the splurge.
  • Narrower, more fun, and better at handling whatever the mountain hands you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Our 75-plus testers put the winter 2026-27 season’s skis, boards, boots, and layers through their paces to find the gear that delivers no matter the condition, from carving skis that tempt you off the groomers to a heated glove worth the splurge.

Narrower, more fun, and better at handling whatever the mountain hands you.

Dynastar M-Cross 88 Frontside Ski.

Salomon S/Pro Alpha C BOA Ski Boot.

Not sure what the mountain has in store? Grab the M-Cross 88 and find out. This ski bridges carving and all-mountain categories and is designed for intermediates leveling up, as well as confident skiers looking to play. Its 14-meter turn radius is just a suggestion—we found it equally as game in moguls and tight trees as on wide-open groomers. Dynastar’s Hybrid Core 2.0 (wood plus polyurethane) delivers a damp, poppy feel no matter the terrain. “It’s a wicked fun carving ski that’s up for a little adventure off the beaten path,” one tester remarked. “It coaxes you into a turn and cradles you there so smoothly I was almost rocked to sleep.”.

According to recent reports, some boots turn heads with new gizmos. The S/Pro Alpha C BOA draws attention with what’s missing: the traditional cuff pivot at the inner ankle. Instead, the cuff flows seamlessly into a low-mounted Powerlink plate—smooth, screw-free, almost Silver Surfer-esque. It’s a radical break from overlap construction, and it delivers two significant wins: shockingly easy entry for a narrow boot, and an on-snow feel like nothing else in the category. That low Powerlink connection creates a direct line from leg to ski—sensitive and reactive enough that we pushed harder into edge angles, hips dropping closer to the snow than in any other boot we tested. This one’s for skiers who want a snug, locked-in fit and live for the high-performance turn.

Recent findings suggest that according to testers, this is the ski your instructor wants you to have. That’s because the Arcade series’ whole mission is high performance made accessible. The women’s Arcade W 88 pulls it off with a full Titanal layer, a power rail down the wood core, and an hourglass sidecut with a wide, rockered tip. The payoff: excellent edge hold and turn initiation so easy it barely takes pressure to roll onto edge and carve. Its flex spans skill differences too—soft enough for intermediates, strong enough for experts. Groomers are its home turf, but this 88-millimeter-waisted ski held its own in bumps and bashed through crud and chop. It’s a fun, effortless frontside ski that can rip or relax.

Five things every skier and rider should already know—but some need to be reminded.

Two boards and a binding engineered to make sketchy conditions feel like solid ground.

Recent findings suggest that revamped for 2027 with input from pro rider Nils Mindnich, the Highpath now features a rounded silhouette that floats better in powder and rides switch better, too. Testers loved the ollie power and reliability of its stiff yet lightweight wood core, reinforced with basalt for snap, and fiberglass to dampen a choppy ride. Responsive and powerful without feeling twitchy, it pairs hybrid camber with a raised flat section underfoot, rockered nose and tail, and a quadratic sidecut for toothy edgehold and fluid carves. One tester called it the “most stable board I’ve ridden.” The stiff flex favors experienced riders, and lighter riders may want to size down.

Sources indicate that feeling tentative about the day’s snow or weather report? The Capita Artemis inspires confidence. Camber underfoot, a directional outline, and a medium-stiff wood core reinforced with flax and aramid strips deliver the edgehold and stability to charge through low-vis moguls, launch side hits, and stick solid landings. This deck prioritizes shooting down the fall line at full speed, making it best for advanced riders. Also available in a women’s model.

Sources indicate that bell-to-bell riders and airtime junkies agree: the Union Neo doesn’t make you choose just one riding style. Its lightweight, mid-stiff highback flex brings heel-to-toe stability without the bulk. EVA-padded ankle straps lock in a cozy, hot-spot-free fit. “Good in any aggressive terrain,” one tester said. “Responsive and strong.” The adjustable baseplate and dual-density bushings soak up everything from overshot park jumps to spring mank, with zero chatter underfoot.

How to initiative a ski vacation that survives a low-snow winter.

These apparel and accessories don’t need sunshine to look—or perform—their best.

Columbia Roffee Ridge Down Jacket.

Industry observers note that the Moiwa is built for mountain mood swings and kept us riding through frigid mornings and stormy afternoons. A two-layer shell pairs nylon made from recycled fishing nets with a PFAS-free waterproof-breathable membrane, while chest and back fleece panels add warmth. The relaxed freeride fit leaves room for two puffies underneath, while pass pockets, pit vents, a powder skirt, and a helmet-friendly hood round it out. It might be overkill for spring skiing, but for resort days during the coldest months, $400 is a score.

Bold style and serious skiing aren’t mutually exclusive. The Slopestar’s flattering barrel-leg design is built on a three-layer 20K waterproof, windproof membrane that handles everything from spring laps to storm cycles. Thigh vents dump heat, RECCO adds peace of mind, and a restroom-friendly side zip simplifies bathroom breaks. Adjustable suspenders dial in the fit, though shorter torsos may find them too long. Introverts be warned: expect lots of compliments in the lift line.

Small upgrades over several seasons have perfected this pant. A fleece-gripped waistband keeps layers tucked, fleece-lined pockets feel heavenly for parking-lot après, and a thigh pocket opens wide enough for a gloved hand to grab a phone or beacon. PrimaLoft Silver insulation handles temps from negatives into the 40s, while ten-inch thigh vents dump heat fast when things warm up. The two-layer waterproof membrane shrugs off snow and sleet. Between the temp range and details, it’s a tough pant to beat for resort days.

Don’t let the svelte look fool you—this cropped puffer earns its keep on the hill with 650-fill down and Columbia’s Omni-Heat Infinity lining that delivers serious warmth without the bulk. Pit zips let heat escape, and soft thumb loops, generous pockets, and a dedicated ski pass pocket round it out—all at a price that doesn’t punish you for wanting to look good.

Sources indicate that milky, overcast skies play tricks on the eyes—unless you’re wearing the Bollé Cerro. Even with the sky spitting snow and rain, we could see 50 feet ahead, and the cylindrical lens delivered a field of view that rivaled goggles twice its size. Flow Tech venting kept things fog-free on the soggiest days. The lens is fixed, not swappable, but its category 1–3 photochromic tech covers most light conditions, so you don’t have to fuss with a second lens. And at $150, they’re a good value.

Industry observers note that sleek is the name of the game for packs that stay out of your way—on the slopes and on the chairlift. The 18-liter Nirvana is slim enough to ride the lift without shrugging it off, yet roomy enough for extra layers, a thermos or water bottle, snacks, and avalanche safety tools in their own dedicated front pocket. Whether you’re lapping the frontside or strapping on skis to bootpack a ridgeline, the Nirvana has your back.

Expensive? Terribly so. Worth every penny? Absolutely. Heating elements run all the way to the fingertips, powered by 22Wh rechargeable batteries for all-day warmth. Paired with a pre-curved leather shell, brushed liner, and low-bulk PrimaLoft insulation, they’re the warmest, most comfortable heated gloves we’ve tested. Haptic feedback makes adjusting heat levels easy, and a magnetic cuff charger simplifies recharging.

Carv 2 won’t replace a real instructor, but it comes close for a fraction of the cost. Clip the sensors onto your boots and the paired smartphone app breaks down your turns—what you did well, what to fix next—pulling data from 1.5 billion tracked turns and real instructor technique tips. This season, the system gets a notable upgrade: an AI coach you can converse with in plain English. It’s not cheap, but compared to lesson prices, it’s a smart investment if you’re stuck in blue square land and ready to chase black diamonds.

Night skiing is the sport’s best-kept secret.

According to recent reports, night skiing gets filed under “kid stuff,” something you age out of, like ski school and hot cocoa bribes. That’s backward. True, night skiing will never hand you the best run of your life. The snow’s usually chalky or refrozen, the lift is a single slow chair, and the terrain is lit like a parking lot. But none of that matters.

There’s a specific, illicit thrill to skiing after dark that goes back to childhood: staying up past bedtime on a school night, bombing down a green or blue run in a full, devil-may-care pizza, feeling like you’ve gotten away with something—you’re outside after dark in the heart of winter, and that alone makes it great.

According to recent reports, it also makes you better. Strip a resort down to one run, and you stop sightseeing and start skiing—really skiing. It’s no coincidence that some of the best alpine skiers in the world were built on hills with just one lift and 300 feet of vertical.

If nothing else, it’s the only time you don’t have to wait in a lift line. Call it kid stuff if you want. Clearly, kids know something the rest of us forgot.
