Breaking: The Best Back-to-School TV Episodes For Every Age

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Timeless back-to-school episodes for kids, from toddlerhood through high school.
  • In a recent development, all good things must come to an end, or so the saying goes, and when you’re a kid that’s never more true than when late August rolls around and summer vacation draws to a close.
  • This is why families sometimes turn to our greatest TV demonstrates for guidance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Timeless back-to-school episodes for kids, from toddlerhood through high school.

In a recent development, all good things must come to an end, or so the saying goes, and when you’re a kid that’s never more true than when late August rolls around and summer vacation draws to a close. Going back to school means an end to unscheduled days of fun in the sun, but it can also be the start of something good. The first day of school can be the first time a kid meets their fresh best friend, or it can kick off an key semester of learning and discovery. It can also be, well, not so good. Sometimes, back-to-school is hard.

This is why families sometimes turn to our greatest TV demonstrates for guidance. TV isn’t the perfect teacher, but it can help families reflect on their own experiences in cathartic ways. Here are 10 of the best back-to-school episodes, an assortment that captures the highs and lows of stepping back into the classroom — or stepping into a latest one for the first time. These episodes are listed here roughly in how young the target audience is for each. So, we’ll start with toddlers and end with high schoolers!

As one might expect from a series based on Mr. Rogers’ Neighborhood, “A Visit to School” showcases the same gentle understanding and straightforward communication the beloved children’s show host excelled at. If you’re feeling scared about doing something latest — like going to the first day of school — talking it out and preparing for the new experience is a great way to feel more confident. It’s actionable advice.

These two Arthur episodes, from the very start and very end of the long-running PBS series, show how every back-to-school comes with its own challenges — and how all of them can be overcome. In the first episode, Arthur and Buster are nervous about their newly introduced third-grade teacher, Mr. Ratburn, until they learn he’s not actually scary at all. Then, 15 real years later, Arthur’s excited to be moving on to 4th grade, until he realizes his best friend Buster won’t be in his class anymore. But, that doesn’t mean that they’ll stop being friends.

According to recent reports, the Disney Channel series Recess is focused on a group of elementary school friends, but not every member of “the gang” was in the first episode. It’s not until the second episode that Gus Griswald demonstrates up at school. Recess has a great way of heightening normal playground politics and Gus’ struggle to escape the “new kid” label is one that anybody who has transferred schools probably empathizes with — and there’s a very happy ending. Not only does Gus get his actual name back and ditch the “new kid” moniker, but he also gets a group of fast friends.

Recess is streaming on Disney+.

The first episode of the Netflix kids' show Karma’s World has the titular character excited about her first day of middle school, only to initially be met with a bully who makes fun of her name Things end up all right, as she makes a friend and the bully eventually apologizes, and the episode offers a more representational take of the back-to-school story.

DJ Tanner’s first day of junior high does not go well, and not just because she’s accidentally dressed just like her teacher, which is just about the least cool thing you can do. She’s also feeling less developed than her classmates, and she only has one class with her friend Kimmy. But, “Back to School Blues” knows that a first day of school is always followed by a second day of school, and DJ (with some guidance for Danny) returns the next day with a good attitude and a little more age-appropriate outfit.

Sources indicate that cory and Shawn’s first day of school is exactly as melodramatic as you’d expect from Boy Meets World, but’s also a pretty heavy look at bullying and brotherly bonds, as Eric stands up for his younger bro even though the “cool” politics of having a younger sibling in the same school as you are fraught, at best. And, Boy Meets World gets to keep the sitcom status quo while also shaking things up with the reveal that Mr. Feely has been promoted to be the principal of their new school.

Most back-to-school episodes are focused, understandably, on the kids who are stepping back into the classroom. But, it’s a big day for parents, too, and this Season 5 episode of Modern Family focuses more on parents Phil and Gloria as they come to grips with the fact that Luke and Manny are growing up!

OK, chances are the average student doesn’t need to list “vampires” as one of their concerns on the first day of school. But, even if Buffy the Vampire Slayer’s premiere episode isn’t as relatable as some of the other entries on this list, it’s still a great back-to-school episode. Sometimes school sucks, and sometimes it sucks blood.

#170581. How To Make Fewer Grocery Trips & Still Eat Well

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1354 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

How To Make Fewer Grocery Trips & Still Eat Well

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1354 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more.
  • It’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks.
  • Industry observers note that the reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more. Experts share how to shop less and still feed your family well.

It’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks. Worse, you then have to play budget Tetris, moving money around to make sure you have funds for the inevitable grocery run you’ll have to make next week. Add in the gas it takes to get to and from, and you’re spent literally and figuratively.

Industry observers note that the reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever. And, sure, cutting back on trips is probably one of the easiest and most logical ways to save money (and time, and sanity). But it begs the question: How long can you go between grocery runs without your family surviving on cereal benders?

We asked food and budgeting experts how they personally make it work.

Most of the experts we polled said one massive shop a week is sort of the sweet spot. “Every extra trip not only takes up valuable time, but is also another chance to grab things that aren’t on the list and drive up your overall grocery bill,” says Laurie Hise, CEO of Passionate Penny Pincher.

Is it possible to stretch it to every two weeks? Maybe. But AJ Prasaguet, head of the iconic Palace bar and restaurant in Miami Beach, points out that biweekly shopping “can work if you have the storage space, freezer capacity, and money available upfront. Those are real considerations, and not every household has all three.”.

Amber Hanson, a licensed nutritionist and founder of Whole You Nutrition, emphasizes that there’s no cut-and-dry, one-size-fits-all answer. Your ideal grocery-shopping cadence will ultimately depend on things like how close you live to a store and when your paycheck hits the bank. If you get paid every two weeks, it might make sense to shop on that timeframe too.

It has been revealed that before you make your little grocery list and head to the store, open up your own fridge, freezer, and pantry. “The best way to save money is to use what you have already paid for,” indicates Hanson.

Jenn Lueke, Latest York Times-bestselling author of Don’t Think About Dinner, does her inventory every Friday night, then builds the next week’s meals around what’s left. Example: “If I know I have a half carton of broth that needs to be used, I’ll make sure to pick up a grain, like rice or quinoa, that I can cook in it.”.

Prasaguet goes one step further. “Give an ingredient its next job before you buy it. If a recipe needs half a container of something, decide where the other half is going.” Take cabbage, for instance. It can be slaw one night, stir-fry the next, and soup filler after that.

Sources indicate that another tip Hise is a fan of is ordering online for pickup or delivery when you can. The simple act of skipping the aisles means you don't have to worry about impulse buys wreaking havoc on your total.

In a recent development, as a busy working mom who regularly feels she has to have everything for the week figured out at all times, this was very liberating to hear! As the experts remind us, life happens. Looks change. A rigid seven-night menu is a fast track to wasted food.

Sources indicate that but if it makes you feel better to have the week mostly lined up, you could follow Hise’s example: strategy five “fresh” dinners a week, leaving one night for leftovers and one for a meal pulled from what’s already in the pantry, fridge, or freezer. Prasaguet relies on a similar formula: four planned dinners, one leftovers meal, one pantry or freezer dinner, on flex night. “That gives the week some structure without pretending everything will go according to plan,” he claims.

Lueke recommends starting with dinners, then exploring how you can make the most of them. “Will the slow-cooker chicken stretch to cover lunches for half the week too? Can I make a double batch of quinoa and bulk up our mid-week sheet pan dinner?” Theme nights like Taco Tuesday or Breakfast for Dinner also help reduce decision fatigue.

The trick to making groceries last, many of the pros explained, is buying foods with different lifespans and eating them in the right order. “You do not want an entire cart of produce that all needs attention at once,” emphasizes Prasaguet.

Lueke thinks about it in three zones:.

It has been revealed that andrea Woroch, a consumer savings expert, notes that some hardy produce (think garlic, potatoes, sweet potatoes, winter squash, even whole apples) can last for months depending on storage conditions as well as how they’re handled. For fast-spoilers like berries, resist the urge to buy the giant fresh packs unless you know your family will gobble them down. Otherwise, stock up on frozen.

If you're afraid frozen and canned food won't pack the same nutritional punch as fresh, well, the experts beg to differ.

“One of the biggest misconceptions about healthy eating is that fresh foods are always better than frozen or canned alternatives. That’s simply not the case,” indicates Jennifer Pallian, a registered dietitian and founder of Foodess. Frozen vegetables are typically flash-frozen shortly after harvest, and research has found they can be just as nutritious as fresh produce that’s been sitting in your fridge for several days. In some cases, they even have more vitamin C.”.

Recent findings suggest that don’t turn your nose up at canned staples, either. Pallian is a major proponent of canned light tuna (a solid source of protein, selenium, and omega-3s) and canned chickpeas, which pack both protein and fiber and are already cooked.

Just opt for low-sodium or no-salt-added canned veggies and beans, and be mindful of foods packed in juices, syrups, or sauces.

Adopting a few little habits can go a long way toward making food last until your next grocery run:.

However, Prasaguet reminds us, “Stretching groceries should never mean stretching food safety.” That means refrigerating leftovers within two hours, eating them within three to four days, or sticking them in the freezer.

According to recent reports, you should know that eating well doesn’t mean you have to buy a bunch of fancy superfoods. “Some of the most nutrient-dense foods in the grocery store are also the cheapest,” Hanson says.

Here’s what our experts say they keep stocked:.

In a recent development, and while many of us think shopping in bulk must save money, Prasaguet notes that it’s “only better value if you can afford it, store it, and finish it.” Hise’s workaround is to grab a few extra cans whenever they’re on sale. “A few extra cans a month can add up to a pantry that carries you through a tight month.”.

If you feel like a failure every time you serve your family dinner out of a bag or can, it’s high time you cut yourself some slack.

“Frozen and canned foods that you actually eat beat fresh vegetables you throw away every time,” notes Hise. Link agrees, adding, “I’d much rather see a family use convenient foods they enjoy than buy fresh ingredients that become a science experiment in the crisper drawer.”.

“A fed family is a win, and ‘fresh’ isn’t the measure of a good dinner," Lueke puts it simply. A balanced meal is made up of a protein, a plant or two, and something filling. It truly does not matter if those came from the produce section or the freezer aisle.

Sources indicate that but maybe Prasaguet sums it up best. “You do not have to prove your love through a complicated dinner,” he reassures. “Feeding your family with the resources you have is already an act of care.”.

#170579. How To Have A Lazy Thanksgiving Without Losing That Holiday Magic

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1021 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

How To Have A Lazy Thanksgiving Without Losing That Holiday Magic

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1021 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Delegate the sides, veto the cranberry sauce, and actually sit down at your own table.
  • As a child, I remember the holiday season feeling like the most magical time of the year.
  • In a recent development, who decorated the house like that?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delegate the sides, veto the cranberry sauce, and actually sit down at your own table.

As a child, I remember the holiday season feeling like the most magical time of the year. Thanksgiving, in particular, seemed like a significant deal because it meant Christmas was right around the corner. The house always felt so warm and cozy with fall decorations on full display — their last hurrah before Christmas took over. And the food. There was always so much delicious food to consume. It was wonderful. It was special. And now, as an adult, I realize it was all thanks to... my mom.

In a recent development, who decorated the house like that? Mom. Who invited the guests and organized the whole Thanksgiving affair? Mom. Who made all of that yummy food? You guessed it — Mom! For me, all of that stuff just seemed to magically get done without much fuss. But there was a fuss. And it wasn’t magic. It was Mom. And now that I’m a mom myself, I realize just how much she had on her plate, figuratively speaking. (Literally, she probably didn’t have much on her plate at all because she was too busy hosting to actually enjoy the meal she created.).

Recent findings suggest that the point is, Thanksgiving can prove to be such a stressful time for moms with all the planning and cooking and putting everyone else’s needs above their own. So much effort is put into making this day perfect for everyone but themselves. But moms deserve to enjoy this holiday too, which is why I say it’s time to invoke a new tradition known as the Lazy Thanksgiving.

Now I know what you’re thinking, but don’t let the name fool you; a Lazy Thanksgiving doesn’t mean a Lame Thanksgiving. There are still plenty of ways to make this day feel special without completely wiping yourself out in the process. Here’s how.

According to recent reports, even if you’re hosting Thanksgiving dinner, that doesn’t mean you should automatically carry the load of the entire meal on your shoulders. Do what any good boss does and delegate an assortment of dishes to other members of the family for them to bring over on the day of. If there’s one thing that you personally enjoy making, then by all means have at it. But everything else should be outsourced to others. Don’t let the burden fall solely on you.

To add a fun twist, reveal that anyone who contributes a dish gets their name entered into a raffle for a special prize at the end of the night. This could be something hassle-free and small, like a cute little ornament or a goodie bag of chocolate. This not only serves as a great incentive to help lighten your cooking load, but it also gives the winner a sweet keepsake of the occasion. (It’s worth noting that this prize part is completely optional — no family member should need to be bribed to help out.).

If you don’t feel comfortable with a potluck approach, but still feel overwhelmed at the thought of making so many dishes, feel free to just simply not make some of those items. (Think of it as a food-ocracy and you’re the president.) Cranberry sauce may be thought of as a Thanksgiving staple, but if only a spoonful or so gets eaten each year, then you are well within your rights to take it off the menu. The same goes for squash or yams or anything else that never ends up feeling worth the effort you put into making it. Odds are, no one is going to care or miss it, and those who do obtain the right to make it themselves.

If you really want to unburden yourself and maximize your relaxation time, you could always get the food from somewhere else and either pick it up or have it delivered right to your door. Honey Baked is always a solid option with great choices for a delicious holiday feast.

It’s more expensive than making it yourself, but a lot less time-consuming, and if various family members chip in to make it happen, it could end up being more than worth the cost. That way you can sit down and actually have time to enjoy everyone’s organization for a change.

Recent findings suggest that do you enjoy cooking but dread the massive clean-up job that comes at the end of it all? Trade in regular dishes and cups for paper ones. Sure, there will still be some dishes to contend with that the actual food was cooked in, but this swap definitely helps cut down on the task and leaves extra room for everything else to go in the dishwasher.

It has been revealed that as a bonus, you can make use of all the extra paper plates by turning it into a fun craft competition for the kids. Whether they use them to make a snowman or some Thanksgiving-inspired creation, this is a great way to get their artistic juices flowing. Choose a family member to be the judge and give out a prize to the winner each year: something like a small toy or maybe even a NeeDoh if you really want the crowd to go wild and can get your hands on one. The kids will love the challenge and look forward to it as part of an annual tradition.

Then again, do you want to go completely rogue? Throw tradition out the window and order takeout or make an easy casserole that will feed everyone and involve zero stress. No turkey. No stuffing. No gravy. No hassle.

However you choose to invoke your “Lazy Thanksgiving,” just make sure that it’s the right fit for you. The whole point is to put less pressure on this day, and by extension, yourself. Remember that less work for you doesn’t equate to a less enjoyable time for everyone else. You being around more, instead of running back and forth to the kitchen, is something the whole family will be thankful for in the long run.

In 1977, the animated version of The Hobbit made a classic book even more powerful than ever.

According to recent reports, back on November 27, 1977, kids watching network TV were introduced to the “greatest adventure” of all time. Although the original Star Wars blew everyone’s minds that summer and forever altered the way we think about blockbuster movies, the Jules Bass and Arthur Rankin Jr. version of The Hobbit quietly pushed the most famous fantasy origin story of all into the mainstream. 45 years later, the impact of the animated Hobbit cannot be overstated.

Recent findings suggest that clocking at just 77 minutes (and apparently, not an hour and a half as many remember it), the animated version of The Hobbit from Rankin and Bass captures the breezy and jaunty quality of J.R.R. Tolkien’s 1937 children’s novel The Hobbit. Of course, even by 1977, The Hobbit had been retroactively relegated to “prequel” status, making it something of an underdog next to the sprawling, and mega-popular Lord of the Rings trilogy of novels, which had been published, originally from 1954 to 1955. Before this, in 1951, Tolkien had revised The Hobbit, to make it more closely aligned with the spirit of The Lord of the Rings, making the slightly more childish version of the book a historical memory.

Bilbo Baggins (Orson Bean) and Gollum (Theodore Isidore Gottlieb) in 'The Hobbit.'.

However, the 1977 animated Hobbit, firmly took the world of Middle-earth and made the adventure for children. With their experiences on other animated kids’ specials like Frosty the Snowman, Rankin and Bass upped their game significantly for The Hobbit, mostly because they had amazing source material to work with. While hardcore Tolkien heads are very aware of the various songs throughout the book versions of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, for the casual viewer in 1977, the staggering amount of music in the animated Hobbit might have seemed weird. However, it was Jules Bass himself who adapted a good chunk of Tolkien’s lyrics directly from the book and then assisted composer Maury Laws, in making it all happen.

It has been revealed that the famous Glenn Yarbrough-sung folksy ballad, “The Greatest Adventure,” was, in fact, the only song that was original to the movie, and not derived from the pages of The Hobbit. This single fact is the microcosm that demonstrates the overall brilliance of this version of The Hobbit; it’s both wildly faithful to the source material, but also morphs into a significantly separate adaptation. Just as Bilbo’s stories of his meeting with Gollum later turned out to be unreliable, the 1977 Hobbit succeeded in turning Tolkien’s book into a modern folk tale. Depending on who was retelling the story, the story could change. Before 1977, this hadn’t happened yet with The Hobbit, and other than Tolkien’s revisions, alternate versions of the story simply couldn’t exist.

Recent findings suggest that as scholars and students of folk tales and fairy tales will tell you; what ensures that a story survives isn’t just the preservation of the text, but instead, the retellings of a story is what creates immortality. In the time before the printed word, this was accomplished through the oral tradition, but in the late 20th century, film adaptations began to do something similar.

Sources indicate that with its unforgettable animation style, brilliant pacing, hilarious moments, excellent casting, and yes, whimsically endearing music, The Hobbit was the first of its kind: A newly introduced take on what had already been an instant classic in 1937. Like the film version of The Wizard of Oz, the 1977 Hobbit sublimated a wonderful kids’ book into a brilliant piece of modern animation. Today, we might think of the 1977 Hobbit as retro. But the reason why it was so important is that, when it comes to amazing fantasy adaptions, the future began right here.

You can rent The Hobbit on Amazon Prime Video right here. It is also included in Fatherly’s 100 Best Kids Movies Ever.
