Eight Sleep’s Alexandra Zatarain on women-centered tech, the science of better sleep, and planning a career around motherhood

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1448 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article is sponsored by Eight Sleep.
  • Alexandra Zatarain helped build Eight Sleep into a tech unicorn, and she’s expecting her first child in January.
  • Meet the expert: Alexandra Zatarain is the co-founder and VP of brand and marketing at Eight Sleep, the sleep-technology manufacturer behind the Pod.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article is sponsored by Eight Sleep. Thank you for supporting the brands that support Motherly and mamas.

Alexandra Zatarain helped build Eight Sleep into a tech unicorn, and she’s expecting her first child in January. Going through pregnancy while running a global firm has reshaped how she sees her own body, her industry and the product she’s building. On this episode of The Motherly Podcast, the co-founder of the sleep-technology company talks about the research that highlighted Eight Sleep’s technology was improving men’s sleep more than women’s and what the company did about it, why sleep is the most crucial thing women can protect, and the career advice she wishes more women heard before becoming mothers.

Meet the expert: Alexandra Zatarain is the co-founder and VP of brand and marketing at Eight Sleep, the sleep-technology manufacturer behind the Pod. The Pod is an intelligent mattress cover that cools or heats each side to your ideal temperature automatically, maximizing deep sleep and minimizing wake-ups. A marketer and brand builder, she grew Eight Sleep from launch into a tech unicorn and helped create what the company calls the sleep fitness movement. Eight Sleep now sells in 37 countries. She’s expecting her first child in January with her husband, Matteo, the company’s co-founder and CEO.

Alexandra Zatarain: So many things. I just turned 37, and I’ve seen so many friends go through pregnancy before me. After my first trimester, I felt so bad, thinking, what a terrible friend I was. When you haven’t experienced it, you have such little empathy for what a woman’s body is going through, especially when life keeps demanding so much of you and it doesn’t stop. I really didn’t understand that you could feel so different in your body for so long. It’s built so much more admiration for women and what we go through, and it’s let me embrace a feminine side of myself that in tech you usually don’t get to bring out.

Sources indicate that alexandra Zatarain: It’s made me realize that the only way the world out there is going to change for our benefit as women and mothers is if more of us are the ones making the decisions. I just don’t see any way around it. We have a lot of parents at Eight Sleep, every executive on our team is a parent, but as a woman the experience is completely different. Unless we can share that first-hand knowledge, it’s going to be hard to make progress as fast as we need to. It’s unfortunate that it takes the first-person experience to become that advocate, because everyone should appreciate what mothers go through, given that we all come from a mother.

Recent findings suggest that alexandra Zatarain: A couple of years ago, our clinical team, which is more than 90% women, was analyzing data from our user base and noticed our technology had been improving men’s sleep more than women’s. They asked, what are we missing in how we design this? It turned out the algorithms that manage temperature while you sleep had been fed more data representing men than women. That’s a classic problem in science, where women are underrepresented because our bodies are more complex. You have to account for where someone is in their hormonal journey, pregnancy, postpartum, perimenopause. So we invested a couple million dollars into research and developed features from it. That changed how we think about ourselves, less about helping everyone in a broad way and more about solving specific problems women have had for ages.

Alexandra Zatarain: Sleep is the most crucial pillar of health. You would die sooner from sleep deprivation than from food deprivation, which tells you how fundamental it is. For women it matters even more because our hormones rule our lives, and sleep is the one tool we have to regulate them. If you sleep well, your chances of better hormonal balance go up significantly. It’s the best medicine we have, more than working out, more than any meal. The challenge is that those same hormones are often playing against us, making it harder to sleep well in different seasons of life, so keeping our routines as stable as possible helps counter what our bodies are going through.

Sources indicate that alexandra Zatarain: The mindset piece is really key. There’s so much going on, the anxiety, the intrusive thoughts, so not being too hard on yourself is the first step. Understanding that the season will pass should put you a little more at ease, because it’s not going to be your life forever. The other piece is setting yourself up with the right systems, and the most important one is available to everyone for free, which is routine. It helps your body a lot. When you do need to sleep, it’ll be easier for your body to fall asleep because it’s used to the schedule.

Industry observers note that alexandra Zatarain: I’m very rigid about my sleep schedule. I travel a lot, so sleep is number one for me. I make space for eight to nine hours every night, and I’m pretty good at hitting it. I go to bed by 9:30 or 10 every single night no matter where I am in the world, and I don’t really use an alarm unless I have to wake up before 6, because my body just wakes up on its own. That schedule is the thing that’s changed my life the most. Second to that is the environment, the temperature in my room and my bed, the lights going dark, no noise.

In a recent development, alexandra Zatarain: I think of myself as an athlete, and we’re all sort of athletes in a way. My sport is making decisions about how to build this business, and that means I have to train, stay healthy and think long term. It’s not a sprint. We’ve been doing this for 12 years, so the question is how do I not burn out and stay here 20 or 30 years more. I’m also lucky I built this with my husband, so there’s no real line between business and personal life for us. It’s all mixed in, but it’s so purpose-driven that achieving that purpose every day is what feeds the energy.

Industry observers note that alexandra Zatarain: I’m very open with them about how intentional I was. I did my embryo freezing in my early 30s because of where I was in life. And I tell them that if they want a career after they have a family, the best time to build equity in that career is to push as hard as you can before. Know what you want, because time isn’t always on our side as women. Move up the ranks, so that by the time you have kids you have more flexibility and maybe a higher income. It is possible, but it takes planning, it will require compromises, and very importantly it will require the right partner.

Alexandra Zatarain: It starts with the people around you understanding what you truly need. Sometimes it’s as simple as the encouragement of, yes, go take a nap, yes, your body’s going through a lot. It gets harder once the baby’s home and the mom is maybe exclusively breastfeeding, because it really all falls on you. So have a strategy in place ahead of time for how the load is going to be shared. Our partners are much more involved than previous generations, so have those conversations early. It doesn’t end with the birth plan. That’s where everything starts.

Alexandra Zatarain: The first trimester was difficult, a lot of nausea, and it was very hard to function at the level I’m used to. I almost never get sick, so feeling sick every day was a huge shift. It put me in the trajectory to build the team that would make it possible for me to become a mother, to figure out what to delegate and who to elevate, and I’ve built a stronger team as a result. But the biggest thing is that it’s taught me to let go. I can’t control how I feel every day. As a Type A person I always want to be in control, and this has been like therapy, learning that I’m not in control of my body. I’m building a human, and it’s fine if for this season things just work differently.

Sources indicate that twenty-four years. That’s how long it had been since I last stood atop a swim block, preparing to dive in for a timed race in an official meet.

A whistle blew. The crowd hushed to silence. A monotone call came over the loudspeaker, “Swimmers, take your mark,” followed by a loud electronic beep that signaled the start of the race. I felt the cold rush of water overtake my body upon diving in. The neurons in my brain feverishly told my muscles to complete the strokes I’d learned decades before. In seconds, it was done. I finished the race.

Recent findings suggest that when I got out of the pool, I walked over to my kids. My son, a competitive swimmer himself, looked at me and earnestly mentioned, “Wow, Mom. I’m proud of you.”.

Like most moms, I have a packed schedule. I work, parent, volunteer at school, shepherd my two kids to practices and social gatherings, throw meals together, walk the dog, and occasionally find a moment to breathe. But over the past couple of years, I watched my growing kids, now ages 12 and 9, discover and engage in passions that light them up. It left me wondering, why not me, too?

“A recurring theme in my practice is women feeling they’ve lost their individual identities somewhere between work, parenting, and meeting everyone else’s needs,” claims Carly Snyder, a Fresh York City–based reproductive and perinatal psychiatrist. “Part of my work involves helping women recognize that their own interests and needs are legitimate.”.

Research highlights a multitude of benefits earned by pursuing hobbies. Hobbyists often have wider social networks, improved mental health markers, and enhanced positive emotions.

According to recent reports, hobbies offer a particularly important lifeline for mothers, who often report losing themselves to the demanding needs of family life. That rings true for Kaitlyn Edington, an art educator and mom of two who recalls struggling after returning to work as a teacher following the birth of her first child. “I was so depleted,” Edington claims. She spent her workdays teaching with short breaks to pump, often bringing her computer into her pumping room so she could catch up on work, then went home to full nights of infant care.

It has been revealed that one day while scrolling on Instagram, Edington saw an artist posting images of her sketchbook paintings. “She changed my life,” Edington says. “Her sketchbook paintings were so loose and free, and she was encouraging people to draw everyday. I remember thinking, ‘If I have to pump two to three times a day, which I absolutely hate, why not pair it with something that I love?’” From then on, Edington sketched when she pumped, and ultimately developed a habit of daily sketching that she continues 10 years later.

Industry observers note that no longer in the pumping phase of life, Edington ensures she gets time to sketch by waking up before her kids. “I hold the habit of waking up before my kids as sacred,” she indicates. “I need that time, when nobody needs me. It’s my emotional rest.”.

According to recent reports, science backs Edington’s belief that her hobby stabilizes her mental health. “Reengaging in meaningful, enjoyable activities can be therapeutically valuable,” Snyder claims. “Behavioral activation, an evidence-based treatment for depression, specifically emphasizes reconnecting with activities that provide pleasure, purpose, or a sense of accomplishment.”.

It has been revealed that snyder has three children, ages 19, 16, and 11, and throughout their lives she has maintained her dedication to skiing, cycling, yoga and running, completing a total of 19 marathons. She knows her kids benefit from her hobbies. Each time Snyder trains for an upcoming marathon, “[My kids] witness my commitment, discipline, setbacks, and perseverance,” she indicates. “Watching a parent pursue a hobby provides opportunities to observe persistence, emotional regulation, problem-solving, and enjoyment.”.

But those benefits are secondary to the impacts hobbies have on the women pursuing them. “I think we’ve become so accustomed to framing everything mothers do in terms of how it benefits their children,” Snyder says. “Women are entitled to happiness and fulfillment for their own sake.”.

Industry observers note that it’s simply an added bonus that when mom is happy for mom’s sake, the benefits for her kids naturally follow, according to multiple studies linking a mother’s well-being with her child’s. Plus, kids also learn that all stages of adulthood, including those under the umbrella of parenting, can include personal fulfillment, curiosity, and growth.

The best way to start a hobby is to let yourself reconnect with something you already love. I remembered how much joy I got out of competing in swim meets in high school, and I was eager to recreate that glee. Ask yourself, “What did I love when I was a kid or a young adult?”.

Sources indicate that your hobby doesn’t have to involve intense commitment. “Reading, gardening, dancing, listening to music, or simply spending time alone can be just as meaningful as running a marathon,” Snyder claims.

Search online for local groups involved in the activity you want to pursue. Your local library may have resources to help you get started as well.

It has been revealed that when you’re ready to commit, set realistic goals. Start by focusing on your hobby consistently for just 10-15 minutes per day. Showing up is the main goal.

According to recent reports, “Motherhood should expand a woman’s identity, not erase it,” Snyder advises. Which hobby will help expand yours?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the lawyer, author, and influencer wants us to talk more and argue less.
  • It has been revealed that if being a parent, a husband, a man, a human has taught me anything at all it’s that communication is everything.
  • It has been revealed that for once, our poor communication is not a product of significant external forces — neither isolationist politics nor overcooked capitalism nor a failing of modern masculinity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the lawyer, author, and influencer wants us to talk more and argue less. He might just be onto something.

It has been revealed that if being a parent, a husband, a man, a human has taught me anything at all it’s that communication is everything. Also, most of us suck at communication.

It has been revealed that for once, our poor communication is not a product of significant external forces — neither isolationist politics nor overcooked capitalism nor a failing of modern masculinity. We can only blame ourselves because, hey, communicating is hard. Getting your point across to a group, your nuclear family, or one single person takes practice and discipline, mistakes and learning. I don’t think we ever get it entirely right.

According to recent reports, well, most of us don’t. There are some communicators in this world that are … blessed. Jefferson Fisher is one such individual. Fisher is a Texan, dad, husband, and personal injury attorney who has made a name for himself through social videos that teach us all how to communicate better.

The videos offer pithy lessons like this: Instead of saying I disagree, “tweak it a little and say, I see things differently.” Why? “When you talk in terms of perspective, you find more connection.” Here’s another: “How I talk to my kids will affect how they talk to their kids.”.

Sources indicate that simple, pointed, and poignant. You can see why millions tune in.

Fisher’s goal is to make people talk more and argue less. It says just that on the cover of his fantastic, practical, wonderfully written book The Next Conversation — a must read for all of us who strive to get along a little better with those around us.

It has been revealed that we caught up with Fisher to talk about his new book and, naturally, anoint him as the latest Cool Dad. Here are some excerpts from our talk, including extras from the Cool Dad Questionnaire and his advice for the most important conversations you’ll ever have.

What’s one thing you wish your kids had today from your childhood?

According to recent reports, probably more of a reckless abandon about what they ate. I grew up in just every Little Debbie from Cosmic Brownies to ... everything you could think of that was probably terrible for us, but we didn't know any different.

What does your partner love about you?

I mean, this is my guess ... I would say what Sierra loves about me is my steadiness. When things don't go to blueprint, I'm pretty rock steady. So when there is something unexpected or the kids go into what we call their midnight madness, when it's right there at bedtime and they're absolutely losing their minds, that's when I'm able to step in and I think I'm able to really notice when she's overwhelmed, and take over.

And what do you think they maybe find annoying about you?

I mean, there's lots. I'm trying to find a really good one like she finds the most annoying about me is sometimes I can be a little bit occasionally of like a party-pooper where the kids are just ... all going nuts and I'm like, "Can we just not yell so much in our house?" So there's that.

Sources indicate that probably the bigger thing she gets more annoyed about is my relationship with money. Its just money. So I'm the spender and so she is the saver. If it's something that's like, "Hey, but this would be fun, even though it's not something we exactly need right now, but it would be a cool memory," I think there's a lot of that.

What does fatherhood mean to you in our current world?

Fatherhood, with the caveat of doing it well to be a good father, I think, is knowing it's a discipline and not a destination. It's a daily devotion to putting your wife, your spouse, your partner, your kids before you. And it's this idea of ... are you inconveniencing them for your comfort or is it the opposite, are you willing to inconvenience yourself for their comfort?

There are times where it's going to be uncomfortable. I don't want to be the one carrying all the bags all the time, but is it what my family needs in that moment in the airport? Yeah, that's what they need. Can I do it? Yeah.

I got to say that the carrying bags all the time is a wonderful metaphor.

Yeah. You're the one that is supposed to shoulder the heavy. So you're supposed to carry what they can't. I'm sure there's a similarity to this phrase of to be what others cannot, you must be willing to suffer what others will not, and so it's like that. To be the dad that others can't, you got to be able to do what others won't.

How do you better communicate with your partner in parenting? Do you think there's ways that you, something that don't apply, or do you follow the advice in your book and have great arguments and conversations with your spouse?

According to recent reports, I wouldn't say there are things that don't apply. I would say what it would need to go deeper on is the theme of repair specifically. So you could have the mindset of arguments and that's something that's very helpful. There's the idea of saying things with control, meaning be regulated and knowing when you need to take that timeout, and using the pauses. But the turn the book doesn't make with regard to marital relationships is repair.

In a recent development, we are talking about words of affirmation, affirming somebody's feelings, being able to take ownership of your words and what that actually sounds like ... how to truly use words of empathy and affirm how they feel, how to say things that are going to bring. We hit on connection in the book, but more in the way of framing non-relationship conversations.

In repair, there is a lot of something as simple as, "Yes, I remarked that. Yes, I did that. I absolutely can see how that would have frustrated you or upset you," or "I think it's totally reasonable for you to feel this way. I don't blame you for being upset about that. I could have done that better." And then how to actually, words of apology, how to repair after a rupture, that to me is, that's a whole different ballgame, whole different set of skills.

Industry observers note that what do you think about checking in? I'm wondering where that falls in the communication line. It's maybe a little bit of the repair, but is that an important thing to do or how do you feel about just what a felt of unspoken understanding between family?

There's an element that my wife and I do and that's check-ins and check-outs. I mean, it's what we call them, things that we do in the morning and things that we do in the evening. Otherwise, there are times you may never talk to your spouse in the day and you know what that's like. Before you know it, you're just two people, somehow there's a woman who lives with me. I don't know who she is, but she's here and you can be roommates that way if you're not checking in with each other. The other is that unspokenness of knowing when something is wrong and that you feel like you might be approaching things from a different vantage. I like asking the phrase, "What's coming up?" "What's coming up for you?".

Instead of me saying, "What's wrong with you" or even, "What's up with you?" That tends to get a pretty defensive response. But if I say something as simple as what's coming up, there's a difference between [that and] saying, "How are you and how's your heart?".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A recent Threads post from @jayonathequeen asked parents for their best “unhinged advice” for raising toddlers, and the replies poured in.
  • Sources indicate that many of the suggestions are surprisingly hinged.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, toddlers are a wild ride. They’re old enough to have opinions, verbal enough to pepper in words like “actually” and small enough to go fully boneless in the cereal aisle when overruled. But with the right frame of mind and a little patience, we can outsmart them.

A recent Threads post from @jayonathequeen asked parents for their best “unhinged advice” for raising toddlers, and the replies poured in. Some came from toddler room teachers, longtime nannies and even doctors. Most came from moms who’ve logged countless hours negotiating with toddlers and consulting their pediatricians. We’ve all earned our stripes, and sometimes there’s nothing like raw mom-to-mom advice.

Sources indicate that many of the suggestions are surprisingly hinged. And certainly no one’s judging.

Anyone who has turned around in a parking lot to find an empty space where a small person used to be knows this particular brand of panic. The thread’s most-liked reply, with nearly 18,000 hearts, went straight at the escape artist problem, and the moms underneath it kept the ideas coming.

Credit: @thriving_out_of_spite, @norcalcaro and @sksargeant via Threads.

One mom’s solution doubled as entertainment.

Credit: @champersstamers via Threads.

(If you try this one, stick with a foil balloon, since popped latex is a choking hazard for little kids.).

Recent findings suggest that toddler palates are a moving target. The food they inhaled one day is suddenly disgusting the next. A couple of moms found that a little creative branding goes a long way, at the table and beyond.

Credit: @analee_inreallife via Threads.

Industry observers note that brushing teeth, putting on shoes, surviving the checkout aisle. The daily stuff is where most battles originate, and, in turn, where moms get the most inventive. A common thread here is giving toddlers a sense of control while you cleverly steer the ship.

Credit: @parentnest.digital via Threads.

Credit: @suziespree via Threads.

And sometimes the smartest move is picking your battles.

Credit: @cryssinikki via Threads.

In a recent development, when a meltdown hits, plenty of moms agreed the first move is regulating yourself. Toddlers take their emotional cues from us, so the calmer we stay, the faster they come back down.

Credit: @sin_standard via Threads.

From there, a little misdirection can work wonders.

Credit: @thenerdyderma via Threads.

Credit: @josephineadel via Threads.

Industry observers note that that sniff trick is a cousin of the viral “Jessica” trick, where a parent interrupts a meltdown by calmly calling for someone who isn’t there. Pediatrician Dr. Madison Szar told Motherly that “What’s that smell?” works just as well, since the surprise is what breaks the loop. Bonus points for the deep breaths.

And for the moments when you’re the one about to lose it, one mom has a suggestion that sounds unhinged until you hear her out.

Credit: @kaitlyn_e.a via Threads.

Then there are the white lies. One bedtime fib stood out as particularly clever.

Credit: @kellywills901 via Threads.

Having raised two kids, one in college and one in high school, I can attest that I lied to them. A lot. The car won’t start unless you’re buckled. It’s against the law to take your shoes off in the store. The toy store is closing, so we have to leave now. I promise you they are both 100% trustworthy, honest people.

When I was a upcoming mom, just 21 and wildly out of my depth, I had a mentor with a toddler of her own. A yoga teacher who became a mom in her early 40s, she was a free spirit who didn’t mother through the lens of anyone else’s scrutiny. It was wild and refreshing.

She was willing to be inconvenienced so her son could explore and held firm when exploring teetered toward danger. She also leaned into the absurdity. At one point she’d somehow acquired a shopping cart, and when her son got grumpy, she’d load him in with a rug, some toys and their cat (I’m not kidding) and march around the neighborhood with the dog following behind.

Sources indicate that toddlers are ridiculous, and we all know it. Sometimes you have to meet the moment with the same.

Industry News: Max Greenfield Is That Dad

📅 14 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1667 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a fresh film, the New Girl star plays a very good dad, naturally.
  • In a recent development, the first thing you may observe about the dad in Netflix’s upcoming teen drama Don’t Say Good Luck is that his hair looks perfect.
  • Greenfield notes that understanding the character was easy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a fresh film, the New Girl star plays a very good dad, naturally.

In a recent development, the first thing you may observe about the dad in Netflix’s upcoming teen drama Don’t Say Good Luck is that his hair looks perfect. That’s only the start of the aspirational cues coming from this character played by Max Greenfield. In this funny — and, yes, tear-jerking — family drama, Greenfield’s character juggles work, elementary-aged twins, a massive-feeling teen, and his wife’s cancer diagnosis. While he is at times off-kilter from all that life throws his way in the film, this dad does not bumble his way through it. In every scene, he finds ways to be the emotionally available parent and partner.

Greenfield notes that understanding the character was easy. “There’s so much of me that’s in that movie,” he tells Fatherly. “I felt so close to what we were doing.” It could be, perhaps, because his daughter, like the main character, is a high schooler; she has mutual friends to the lead actress, Sunny Sandler; and her experience — at least onstage, navigating high school life — just resonated.

We sat down to give Max Greenfield the Cool Dad questionnaire, and then talked about the movie, finding patience, and fighting parental anxiety — and why LA’s bagels are seriously underrated.

This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Recent findings suggest that I finished watching Don’t Say Good Luck today. I definitely did some crying.

They keep playing clips in these interviews that I’m doing for press, and they’ll play it before the interview, and I’m constantly like, “I need a minute.”.

Industry observers note that it’s intense. It’s a wonderful film. I’m wondering how close of a dad are you to who you play on screen in Don’t Say Good Luck. Are you that dad?

I mean, there’s so much of me that’s in that movie. I felt so close to what we were doing. It was really the reason I wanted to do it. My daughter, I think, is a year younger than Sunny [Sandler, the lead], and I was really aware that this was going to be a movie that Sunny was starring in. And from everything that I had heard, I had never done a Sandler movie before, but his sets are famously the best. And so I really wanted to just make sure that she had a comparable experience on this with somebody else. I felt like I knew how to do that.

Sources indicate that my daughter and her have mutual friends, I know where she goes to school… just a lot of the stuff I just was like, “I know this world well.” And so talking to somebody like Sunny is not an issue for me. And trying to be light and supportive in this environment, it was something I felt like I was capable of doing. I didn’t know if I was going to be very good in the movie as an actor, but I was like, “I think I know how to be the dad.” And then there’s the two young boys in the movie, the twins, and they were so funny because they were just never acting. They just were running around.

They’re a little bit younger than my son, but I just coached my son’s basketball team, and wrangling all those kids and getting them going, getting them involved, it was very good prep work for dealing with these two boys. And it made the scenes and made the movie so much fun.

Yeah. Everything was just like, “Oh, this is what my real life is.” And being there with Sunny, I understood that relationship. Being there with the boys, I was like, “I get this relationship.”.

Recent findings suggest that there was a more dramatically real scene later in the movie … I personally had a similar experience to the lead character. My mom had cancer when I was a sophomore in high school, and all I could think about was how I wanted you — your character — to be my dad for that time. For example, that scene when you were sitting in the car and Sunny asked, “Are you okay?” And you asked, “Are you okay?” And both of you said, “No.” It was just… right.

According to recent reports, that was a really cool scene. Julia Hart, who had directed the movie and wrote the movie along with Laura Hankin and Jordan Horowitz … [had] a lot of conversations about that scene, and they were so generous in my input. It really felt like that scene was going to be the scene for this relationship. And as we started to see how the movie was playing out and what was happening before then, we had sent a bunch of drafts of that scene back and forth to one another, and we all collectively landed in that spot because it really needed to set up everything that comes after that, but it needed to honor everything that was built up before it, and it needed to feel real.

I didn’t want there to be an answer or a fix to what was happening, but I wanted them to feel it, both characters. When we shot that scene, it was nuts. It was really heavy, man.

Industry observers note that in this movie, you run a bagel shop. So what’s your order?

Oh, wow. Great question. I’ve probably gotten older and more healthy than I need to be, more LA than I need to be. I’ll give you two. One’s an everything bagel [with] just cream cheese, onion, tomato, lox.

That can’t ever miss, it’s the best. The other one is … either a light cream cheese spread [or] the right type of hummus and then just veggies. But fresh, good veggies that are with the right type of dressing on it and salt and pepper. There’s a place in LA that has been hyped and hyped and I finally went there, I don’t know, a month or two ago. It’s called Courage Bagels. And the line is a mile long. And I was like, “I’m not waiting in line.” And then my daughter and I were like, “Let’s go wait in line.” So we went over there and they had one, I think it’s called the Garden or something. I don’t know. Holy sh*t. It was unbelievable.

It has been revealed that one of the major themes of the movie I wanted to get your take on is disclosure to children. That is, what you tell a kid, what you don’t tell a kid, when you’re protecting them from the truth, and when that backfires. I was just wondering if you had thoughts on how you strike that personally.

In a recent development, it’s a really good question. I actually feel like I’ve done a good job with this, personally. There are certain things that I want them to discover on their own, and hopefully my job is to have created a space where they feel comfortable to then bring those things up to me. And then depending on how the question’s asked or how much they want to know, you ease them into certain topics of discussion and what you choose to discover based on what they’re asking. And you let that conversation be ongoing. And so I’ve had some real good success in some areas where those conversations have opened up and become more in-depth over time. And as a result, I see that my kids are way more comfortable with information that I was worried might be confusing or scary. And because they’ve sort of been able to take it in at their pace.

How has your outlook changed now that you’re past the baby and elementary parenting and you have a 16- and 11-year-old?

According to recent reports, I’m making a lot more mistakes. That thing we talked about, responsibility versus what to let go, that line is thinner and thinner every day. And there’s so many times where, what are the things that I feel like I need to control to make me feel safer in this situation that is so scary? And being a fear-based parent is not a good zone to operate from.

It has been revealed that and so it’s like my daughter’s now driving and she gets her driver’s license and it’s just like, my wife and I are both like, “Well, so the next day, is she just driving to volleyball practice? Is that how that works?” And if you strip all the fear away from it, you’re like, “Yeah, she practiced and worked up to it and has now passed the test and she’s allowed to legally drive. So yes, why wouldn’t she be able to?” There’s a period of time when they’re small where you’re like, “Yeah, this is just going to keep getting better.” And then it shifts in the most terrifying way and you’re like, “Oh, this is all so much worse.”.

Recent findings suggest that when we were [learning to drive], I would sit in the car with her, we would drive, and I would go, “Oh, you know what? All the anxiety and fear I have about the future and life and work and all the nonsense, that’s not real.” When I’m sitting in a car with my daughter and she’s driving, this is real fear. This is what real fear feels like. It’s like, this is the shark in the water kind of fear. And it’s heavy and it’s tangible. And you almost hold it and you go, “This is what real fear feels like, and this is appropriate for the situation.” So outside of that, when I do feel any sort of anxiety about the future or whatever it is, I go, “Oh, this is not real.” And now I know the difference. So at least I have that.

Nick Viall on love, life, and being a twin dad.

Industry observers note that nick Viall first appeared on “The Bachelorette” 12 years ago and ever since, he’s had one serious reality TV run. From “Bachelor in Paradise” to “Dancing With the Stars,” “The Masked Singer” to “Age of Attraction,” which he right now co-hosts with his wife, Natalie Joy Viall , his handsome mug is everywhere. He also notably doles out relationship advice, also alongside his wife, on the The Viall Files, one of the most popular relationship podcast on Apple that airs three to four times a week.

What viewers might not know is that this Wisconsinite, the second oldest of 11 siblings, has a two-year-old and, since July, twin infants. So how’s twin dad life? “When you tell people you're expecting ... people are more prone to just kind of, I call doomsday kind of advice,” he tells Fatherly. “And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing.” We caught up to give Nick the Cool Dad questionnaire and it seems he didn’t want it to end. “It's fun to talk about fatherhood,” he claims. Which is good, because he’s got a lot of fathering on his hands right now.

Sources indicate that how's being a twin dad going? I have had friends who were twin parents, and it's so … much.

According to recent reports, overall, it's great. I mean, I think every stage is different. With newborns — it sounds like you're a father as well, so as you know — they're just little potatoes at first. And for the most part, other than the regular feedings and having to wake up multiple times in the middle of the night, which can get tiring, it's not too bad. But obviously those moments … pockets of overwhelmingness of like, "Oh, no." One cries, and then you calm one down, and then another one cries.

In a recent development, for the most part, I was joking with Natalie, my wife, about it honestly, because you get so nervous about twins. A lot of times when you tell people you're expecting ... People are more prone to just kind of give what I call doomsday advice where it's like, "Oh, get ready for hell," or something like that. And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing For the most part, it just feels like you got a BOGO, like a buy one, get one free. And it's like, great. Obviously, my wife during the pregnancy, different experience. Obviously, I think it's a lot more on mothers to carry two than one.

But it's been really exciting to just be like, "Oh, we already have three kids, and it only took two pregnancies." So easy for me to say, obviously, but it's been really fun.

It has been revealed that well, congratulations. The first question I have is just wondering what kind of dad are you?

I'm a pretty involved dad and pretty hands-on. Natalie and I, ever since we've been together, we just share the responsibilities of our household. And that was true even before we became parents. I was lucky enough to have the parents I had. And I think that the biggest takeaway I had from my childhood is just how my parents worked as a team.

It has been revealed that I have 10 brothers and sisters. And my parents were very lower middle class, very blue collar. My mom stayed home and worked. I mean, my mom stayed home and raised the kids, my dad worked, but that wasn't based on some kind of a decision they made. It was more like that was the situation they had.

It has been revealed that in terms of the day-to-day, they shared their responsibility. My mom did a lot of the traditional day-to-day keeping up the house, but my dad would often make dinner. My mom sometimes would mow the lawn. It was just more like all hands on deck type of thing, and you just do things as a team. And that's just something Natalie and I implemented into our relationship early on. And then, obviously, when River indicated up, it continued. And then Natalie started working with me on the show.

And so really we're just very involved. And so any little thing I can do to help Natalie or just be an involved parent, we're doing things together every step of the way.

Sources indicate that so I'm just hyper-involved. There's no her thing, my thing. We conquer and divide, and certainly, we joke where I'm allergic to laundry, she's allergic to dishes. I don't mind doing dishes. She doesn't mind doing laundry. So there's definitely things that we have our preferences, but for the most part, we just share everything.

Nick Viall and Natalie Joy Viall have many joint ventures including, namely, the uber-successful Viall Files relationship advice podcast.

What's one thing you wish your kids had today from your childhood or will have?

Recent findings suggest that well, I feel very fortunate to say that I was lucky enough to try to be able to give the best part of my childhood to my children because I was lucky enough to buy back my grandfather's lake house a couple years ago. And that was a place that in my childhood was like my Nirvana. It was my special place.

Sadly, when my grandfather passed away when I was in the fourth grade, they sold that property, and it was like this devastating moment of my life. It was like some real childhood trauma.

And it was a place that, quite frankly, I had recurring dreams all the way into adulthood. And again, I was lucky enough to buy it back and just really excited that it will be a place that I'll hopefully be able to give to my children, and a place that they'll be able to grow up and we'll have, obviously, a lot of hopefully monumental family events there. So that's definitely something I want them to have.

Recent findings suggest that but thinking in the vein of how times might be different, I think the world's changing so fast. I have such fond memories of going to the movies as a child, going to Blockbuster and picking on a movie and things like that. And some of those moments I hope we'll still be able to do. Or just maybe I hope there's a renaissance of people wanting to get outside, touch grass type of thing. And I hope that's something our children will be able to enjoy.

Industry observers note that and certainly, in the lake houses up in the middle of nowhere in Wisconsin will be a great tool to help our kids want to be outside and play in nature and just make-believe. Most of my childhood was a lot of just make believe with my friends outside. And we would ride our bikes all over the place.

Recent findings suggest that it's weird. I'm sure you're probably familiar with that book, The Anxious Generation by Jonathan … he talked about the freedoms that kids used to have back in the day and parents like 5, 10 years ago got a little... it's like you get nervous about the world, but you took for granted, again, the dangers of the phone. And so I'm really hoping my kids get to embrace the world and get outside and play make believe with their friends and things like that. So that's a massive focus for us and certainly, hopefully, something that I hope they do get to enjoy because those are always fond memories that I have as a child.

In a recent development, that's a great perspective. I mean, I do agree that right now is a good time to have kids because everyone is much more aware of the difficulties parents are facing . You'll see all the support in elementary school. It's really talked about a lot.

And on to the next question: What does your wife love about you?

Industry observers note that well, I think probably just the fact that, I hope, that I like to think I'm her rock. There's so much burden and pressure on moms postpartum. I like to think that my job is just to be a cheerleader. When I get a sense that she's stressed out or feeling overwhelmed, I'm quick to try to give her a break, tell her to go lie down if that's what she wants to do. I'm always there and always available.

Recent findings suggest that and I hope that's one thing that she loves most about me, but I just try to be as supportive as possible just to remind her and just be a cheerleader. Just always remind her that she's doing a great job because, again, there's just so much pressure that moms put on themselves.

The other side of that coin, what does she maybe find annoying about you?

Oh, my God, the list is so long. Well, I don't know how to close a cupboard. I don't put things away. I leave a trail of destruction wherever I go. I'm messier than our two-year-old. So there is that.

It has been revealed that I've recently got back into some video game playing, which definitely gives her the ick, but she is kind enough to let me decompress with a game here or there. So I think she'd prefer it not to exist, but … everything in moderation. Again, the trick for any dad out there who enjoys a video game or two is to never let it get in the way of being helpful. So that's the trick to get it in when you can, but never let it come in the way of, obviously, being a partner and being a father.

What does fatherhood mean to you in the current world?

Sources indicate that I mean, it means everything to me. I've had this conversation with a lot of peers that I have, and I have a lot of women friends in the space I work in, and so talked to some fresh young mothers, young professionals who, obviously, their careers are and still are really key to them.

Sources indicate that once you have a child, I describe it as the easiest North Star. I've been fortunate enough in my life to accomplish a lot of cool things and it's nice to have individual accomplishments and accolades and awards, but they're not always as fulfilling as you think they might be when they happen. Fatherhood, parenthood is just... you always know why you're doing something. You always know what the purpose is. And so even the late nights, it's a drag to get up at 2:00 in the morning, but you know why you're doing it, and you always get a sense of purpose and accomplishment. And it's just the best motivator. No matter what's going on in work or in our personal life, it really calms you down.

I'm a fairly anxious, high-stress guy. It's easy for me to get worried about work and all the things that are going on in this world. And then I have the benefit of coming home, and especially with River now when she greets me. I'm constantly on my phone with work, and I'm never not working in a sense, but when I walk into the house, Natalie's incorporated this kind of best practice of making sure I'm off my phone and I'm very present to greet River. Even if it's for a few minutes, even if I still have some work left to do, I never walk in on the phone and I'm not giving her my undivided attention. And it's something like Natalie incorporated, which I really appreciate that she did, and I think it's just a really great best practice that we do.

Thank you so much for all the thoughtful answers.

I appreciate it, man. It's fun to talk about fatherhood.

According to recent reports, it's something I really enjoy. And it's weird because in my... I don't know if you've noticed this. I mean, it's weird how parenting has become, like everything else these days, almost like a polarizing topic. No parent is indifferent about parenting, and obviously, every parent comes with passion, but it's weirdly become a topic that I'd want to talk about more, but sometimes it's like you want to be careful because you don't want to force your thoughts and feelings onto others.

How to thank school support staff this American Education Week (Hint: It’s not a mug)

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (604 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, my son’s favorite person in elementary school was the nurse.
  • Industry observers note that that nurse lovingly cared for kids who needed far more support than my son did.
  • People like her have a name in education circles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, my son’s favorite person in elementary school was the nurse. She was warm and welcoming, always quick with a comforting hug. More importantly, she had the best Band-Aids in the building, and she wasn’t stingy about giving them out. A scraped knee got one. So did a paper cut, and even some invisible injuries, too. She knew when a kid headed to see her, it wasn’t necessarily about needing that Band-Aid.

Industry observers note that that nurse lovingly cared for kids who needed far more support than my son did. There were kids who came to her office with a belly ache that wasn’t a stomach bug, but because they hadn’t had breakfast, and possibly dinner either. There were kids who could barely stay awake in class because they’d spent the night in a car instead of a bed. She met those kids with the same warmth she gave my Band-Aid collector, and I’m certain she kept a stash of snacks in her desk for those visits in particular.

People like her have a name in education circles. They’re education support professionals, or ESPs, and they include school nurses, cafeteria workers, bus drivers, security staff, paraeducators, technical personnel, custodians, skilled trade workers, and front office staff. Ask kids about their favorite grown-up at school, and there’s a decent chance the answer is one of them.

In a recent development, the people our kids adore are often the people schools pay the least. Nearly 32% of full-time ESPs earn less than $25,000 a year, according to the National Education Association, and on average, they’re paid below a living wage in all 50 states.

Sources indicate that that’s not a livable wage in most areas. “Our wages are so low, we are forced to have two or three jobs,” paraeducator Yahaira Rodriguez told NEA Today. The nurse who stays late with a hungry kid may be heading to a second job after school, eating dinner in the car on the way. That’s a long day for someone whose job is to take care of everyone else’s kids. It also makes it hard to stay in the job. Before the 2024–25 school year, 69% of public schools reported trouble filling at least one non-teaching position, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. That means the kids who rely on them the most are the ones who lose out when they leave or the positions can’t be filled.

In a recent development, the NEA ESP Bill of Rights lays out what these professionals need to stay in the jobs our kids depend on. Developed by ESPs themselves, it asks for pay that covers the bills without a second job, health care they can afford and a workplace ‘free of violence, including physical, verbal, and emotional abuse.’ It’s a practical document about what it takes to keep these jobs filled. The full list includes:.

Since the movement began, 18 states have launched ESP Bill of Rights campaigns, according to NEA.

Industry observers note that american Education Week runs November 16 to 20, 2026, and this year NEA is using it to honor education support staff. Here are a few ways to show up for the people who show up for our kids:.

Recent findings suggest that our kids won’t remember most of what happened at school, but they’ll remember who was kind to them there. For a lot of them, that’s a nurse, a cafeteria staff or a bus driver doing the job on less than a living wage. Sign the ESP Bill of Rights pledge and help them stay.

#170468. Industry News: E-bike safety for kids: What pediatric ER doctors want parents to know before gifting one

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1093 w)

Industry News: E-bike safety for kids: What pediatric ER doctors want parents to know before gifting one

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1093 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • E-bikes and e-scooters have become a hot item on holiday and birthday wish lists.
  • It has been revealed that if you’re trying to decide whether or not to give your kid an e-bike, it helps to know what pediatricians are seeing in their emergency rooms.
  • According to recent reports, I talked with two physicians who’ve treated these kids, Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

E-bikes and e-scooters have become a hot item on holiday and birthday wish lists. They’ve also become a hot topic in online forums and parenting circles, where people constantly worry about kids on e-bikes going too fast, losing control or making poor choices. I’ve seen it myself on my city’s bike path—kids flying by and recklessly weaving past pedestrians and other cyclists.

It has been revealed that if you’re trying to decide whether or not to give your kid an e-bike, it helps to know what pediatricians are seeing in their emergency rooms. A JAMA study published in November 2026 looked at more than 13,000 injury visits for kids under 18 at six large U.S. children’s hospitals between 2023 and early 2026. E-bike injuries grew 33% per quarter over that stretch and e-scooter injuries grew 15% per quarter, compared with 2% for traditional bikes and 4% for traditional scooters. About a quarter of the e-bike injuries and nearly half of the e-scooter injuries involved kids under 12.

According to recent reports, I talked with two physicians who’ve treated these kids, Dr. Beth C. Natt, system medical director of pediatrics at Atlantic Health, and Dr. Zebulon J. Timmons, division chief of emergency medicine at Children’s Nebraska in Omaha, about what parents should weigh before buying one and how to keep kids safer if one is already in the garage.

“It mostly comes down to speed,” Natt indicates. “Doubling the speed roughly quadruples the force in a crash.” Some e-bikes can top 25 mph, and Natt notes that e-bike crashes are far more likely to involve a car.

Timmons points to the rider as much as the bike. “Kids do not have the frontal lobe capacity and reaction time to make judgments at that speed,” he indicates. “You don’t take your young child to the batting cages and have them start at 80 mph.”.

It has been revealed that in the JAMA study, 17% of e-bike injuries led to a hospital stay, the highest share of any group of injuries, and 10% involved a brain injury, double the rate for regular bikes. Severe injuries, like those needing ICU care or surgery to fix a fracture, were twice as common on e-bikes, too (8% vs. 4%). Natt mostly sees broken wrists, arms and legs, plus head, face and dental injuries. Timmons sees a lot of open fractures, where the bone breaks through the skin. “Kids’ heads are bigger relative to their bodies, so they tend to hit head-first,” Natt claims, “and a fracture through a growth plate can affect how a bone grows later.”.

Recent findings suggest that the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) notes kids under 16 shouldn’t ride e-scooters and, citing Consumer Product Safety Commission guidance, no e-bikes for kids under 12. Timmons says kids 12 to 15 can ride a Class 1 e-bike with proper safety training and gear, and teens 16 and up can consider a Class 2, though many will still be safer on a Class 1. Natt is more conservative. “Most pediatric injury experts would say no throttle-powered e-bike or e-scooter before about 16, and some argue for 18,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that A child is ready, Natt says, if they can handle a regular bike confidently in traffic, follow the rules when you’re not around, wear a helmet without reminders and judge how fast cars are coming. “Most kids don’t have that judgment until at least their teens,” she notes.

Recent findings suggest that class 1 e-bikes are pedal-assist only, up to 20 mph. Class 2 adds a throttle, still capped at 20 mph. Class 3 is pedal-assist up to 28 mph, and many states restrict it to riders 16 and older. For kids, choose Class 1 and skip the throttle, Natt notes, and avoid “e-motos” sold as e-bikes, since they go much faster. Both doctors note a regular pedal bike is still the safest choice for most kids.

There’s no federal minimum age for e-bikes, and more than half of states set age limits for Class 3 models, so check your state and town’s rules before you buy.

According to recent reports, timmons claims a standard bike helmet is fine up to about 15 mph. From 15 to 25 mph, he recommends a helmet certified to the NTA 8776 e-bike standard, and above 25 mph, a motorcycle or moped helmet. A full-face helmet adds protection for the face and jaw, Natt says, and any helmet should be replaced after a crash.

According to recent reports, keeping it on is another matter. Timmons states fewer than 25% of kids treated in pediatric emergency departments were wearing a helmet when they crashed, and many take them off once they’re out of a parent’s sight. Make wearing a helmet a non-negotiable, and let friends and neighbors know to keep an eye on your child. If they’re spotted without the helmet, the bike goes away.

After the helmet, wrist guards and gloves help most because broken wrists are so common, Natt says. Front and rear lights plus reflective clothing help drivers see your child. Timmons recommends that kids wear closed-toe shoes (“No Crocs”), and for teens 16 and up on a Class 2, motorcycle-style long pants and sleeves.

It has been revealed that any head injury or neck pain after an e-bike or e-scooter crash should be checked in the emergency room, Timmons indicates. Natt says to go if your child passed out, even briefly, or keeps vomiting, or has a worsening headache, confusion, unusual sleepiness, a seizure, weakness or numbness, belly pain, a limb that looks bent or can’t bear weight, or a deep cut or facial or dental injury.

Watch for “handlebar injuries,” too, when the handlebars turn sideways and strike the chest or belly. “This mechanism causes all the force to be delivered to a small area and can cause significant internal injuries,” Timmons claims. A handlebar-shaped bruise on the chest or abdomen means a trip to the ER. Once there, tell the care team what kind of e-bike your child was riding and whether they wore a helmet, Natt says.

Industry observers note that if the e-bike or e-scooter isn’t right for your child’s age, consider exchanging it, Timmons says, or look for a community buy-back program. “This last trauma season was the worst one in my career and that was largely driven by e-bike/scooter injuries,” he says.

“These are motor vehicles, not toys,” Natt indicates. “A crash at e-bike speed can look more like a motorcycle injury than a bike injury.”.

Nate Bargatze Is (Sort Of) Leading By Example

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Though he’s one of the biggest comedians in the world, Nate Bargatze’s career path was anything but straightforward.
  • According to recent reports, it’s a bit hard to believe that Nate Bargatze, one of the biggest comedians today, met his wife while working at Applebee’s in Tennessee.
  • Recent findings suggest that but authenticity matters to him, in his storytelling and what he’s learned over the years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though he’s one of the biggest comedians in the world, Nate Bargatze’s career path was anything but straightforward.

According to recent reports, it’s a bit hard to believe that Nate Bargatze, one of the biggest comedians today, met his wife while working at Applebee’s in Tennessee. Or that on his first job overseeing the dog kennel in an amusement park (apparently a thing), he let the dog out (“it was a whole thing … and that was kind of the end of the dog kennel”). Or even the basic fact that at the height of his career he decided to move back to Tennessee so that his teen daughter might have a more normal life. Bargatze’s life, like his comedic work, reads like a folksy tall tale. It draws you in with the details and lulls you with its sense of warmhearted authenticity — then lands a punchline.

Recent findings suggest that but authenticity matters to him, in his storytelling and what he’s learned over the years. He recently brought some of his experience to Ford’s Accelerate conference, where he is a spokesperson for what they’re calling the “essential economy” — of skilled technicians and tradespersons, a group that, according to economists, is in short supply and needs to grow. Bargatze is an interesting choice for this forum, a comedian with a high school degree and no formal trade skills besides those he learned onstage. He went to community college for a year and worked a variety of jobs, from waiting at Applebee’s to reading water meters. But he gets the value and opportunity in trade school. “I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools. I did not go to college ... They’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, notable for just the future.”.

Nate Bargatze poses with students at the Ford Accelerate conference, which he mc-ed.

Sources indicate that he also is thinking about this because his 14-year-old is not too far from entering the workforce. “Right now it’s like, yeah, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it. But then, as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room, so you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to [instill that urgency] as a parent. And if you don’t, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you.” Which all boils down to a most authentic parenting philosophy: “Be a good example, basically.”.

Tell me about what you’re doing right now at this Ford Accelerate event.

According to recent reports, what Ford is doing with this event that we’re at right now, where they’re showing kids going into trade schools ... letting kids know that this is kind of the future, that they’re going to have jobs. And it’s like we don’t know where jobs are going with AI and all this stuff, but the trade schools… We need that. I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools.

According to recent reports, I worked the water meters. I did not go to college. They’re going to get more college than I did. But they’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, key for just the future. I think they’re putting themselves in such a great position, probably better than they realize now, but they’re going to, I think, look back and just be like, “Man, that was such a good call.”.

I’m wondering, since we’re talking about work, what’s the most key thing you’ve learned about work in your life?

I always go back to when I waited tables at one point and our manager there always talked about a sense of urgency. And that’s always stuck with me for some reason. It was just going to a table and just have a sense of urgency. It goes a long way when you get to that table and they really feel like they’re being taken care of. I think I’ve just kept that even as I’ve gone forward. If you respond to emails or my team is talking to you, I don’t want to be like, “I’ll get to them next week.” You kind of want to just be like, “No, let’s get to them and let’s make sure that we stay on top of it.”.

Nate Bargatze plays an off-the-rails George Washington when he hosted SNL in 2024.

Speaking of people who don’t have it, how do you instill that sense of urgency in your kid without them fighting back?

Industry observers note that you say stuff as a parent, you don’t know what’s sticking and what’s not sticking. You keep talking about it, and the older she gets — she’s 14 now — the more she’s going to see examples of it. Right now, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it, but then as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room. So you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to do it as a parent. And if you don’t do it, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you. And so, be a good example, basically.

Then what’s one thing you wish your kids had today that you had during your childhood?

I think not the internet, maybe. That would be something, even though it’s great and the connection and it’s all this stuff, you just wish they would’ve had a little more... I think innocence lasted longer when we grew up because you just weren’t pounded with information all day long.

What’s your wife love about you?

Recent findings suggest that I hope me for being me. We’ve been together before any of this started. We met at Applebee’s. Our 20th wedding anniversary is Oct. 13. I think it’s taking time to get used to it, but we’re along this ride together and just the surprises. We don’t know where everything’s going to end up or what’s going to happen. I think that she sees that I work hard at stuff and has been behind the scenes and loved me before any of this and loves me now. So it’s just to have the support from her, I wouldn’t be here without her. And she very much kept me grounded in a world when you come up in comedy that you could not be... It’s easy to not be grounded.

On the flip side, what do they maybe find annoying about you?

She doesn’t like eating near me because she thinks I’d chew loud. I don’t think I’m too loud. I think it’s very normal. But she gets very uncomfortable if she’s like... I mean, if she’s on the couch and I’m at the table right behind the couch, she cannot stand it. So I eat outside now — and I only do soups.

It has been revealed that what kind of dad are you? How would you describe yourself as a dad?

Recent findings suggest that I like to be... You find moments to talk to your kid. As they get older, they have friends. She’s young and all that, so they want to run with their friends. A significant part is finding the moments of when they can get very talkative, and so you can find these little pockets and really try to home in on those.

Industry observers note that she knows I’m a fun time. She can take me for a ride, where her mom can put her foot down a little bit more. She knows where to go. She thinks very much like me, and she can work you if she wants something, and she works me quite a bit.

Coming back to the work thing, what was your first job?

My first job, I worked at Opryland Theme Park in Nashville. I was 15, and so I was a sweeper. I walked around and just swept up the park. And I also did the dog kennel. After the sweeper, I got promoted to dog kennel.

Nate Bargatze with his wife, Laura Bargatze.

Well, because people would bring their pets because they’re on vacation and they’d travel with their pets.

Recent findings suggest that so you can’t bring them to the park. And so people would bring their dogs in or whatever, their cats. I think we had a chicken. People travel with some weird animals. But one dog got out, and so it was a whole thing. And that was kind of the end of the dog kennel. I think I went back to sweeping after that. But he got out, and so we had to call the... again, pre-internet, so you got to announce to the park, “Whose German shepherd got out in the parking lot?” And then they got to go search for this dog and it was under a parked car. And yeah, I still talk to that family today.

I’m sure you don’t. They don’t want to talk to you.

Recent findings suggest that no. But I bet they still remember it. We both still remember that.
